Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 11, to amend the Interest Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the Interest Act as it now stands does not place any limit upon the rate of interest that may be agreed to or that may be collected. Section 1 now reads:
Except as otherwise provided by this or by any other act of the Parliament of Canada, any person may stipulate for, allow and exact, on any contract or agreement whatsoever, any rate of interest or discount which is agreed uipon.
The bill which I am introducing proposes to place a limit of seven per cent per annum upon the rate of interest that may be charged and collected. It also contains another provision which would limit the rate of interest which might be collected on mortgages on real estate to four per cent per annum.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it desirable that I should read a short statement to the house in connection with the celebration of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the king's accession to the throne:
As announced in the speech from the throne, Canada will join with the rest of the empire in celebrating on May 6th next the 25th anniversary of the king's accession to the throne. In accordance with His Majesty's

expressed wish that all unnecessary expenditure should be avoided and that celebrations should be local, the government will not initiate any great national celebration.
It is proposed that the day will be celebrated as a public holiday throughout the dominion, and that a salute shall be fired at Ottawa and at all provincial capitals.
The government will announce a program of proceedings to take place in Ottawa on Parliament Hill on the morning of May 6th, which will enable members of representative national and' local patriotic organizations, school children and the public to join in commemorating the king's silver jubilee. His Excellency the Governor General will attend, and will present His Majesty's silver jubilee medals to those of our fellow-citizens in Ottawa, to whom they are awarded.
The lieutenant-governors of the several provinces will be invited to carry out in the provincial capitals programs similar to that which will be adopted at Ottawa. Mayors and reeves of civic and municipal centres, other than Ottawa and the provincial capitals, will be invited to organize local celebrations on similar lines.
Members of the defence forces will be free to participate in any functions arranged by local authorities.
As a special act of thanksgiving on the part of the people of Canada on the occasion of this anniversary, His Excellency the Governor General, on March 1st, will initiate an appeal for the establishment of a permanent fund, to be known, by His Majesty's gracious permission, as the "King George V. Silver Jubilee Cancer Fund for Canada." An opportunity will thus be afforded to every household that is able and willing to contribute to participate in providing a permanent Canadian fund which will promote the welfare of our people in memory of this great historic occasion in the history of the British empire.
In due course it is proposed that both houses of parliament shall submit a loyal address to His Majesty the King.

Hon. R. B. HANSON (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Precious Metals Marking Act, 1928.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-" Mount."

Perhaps I should give a brief explanation of the bill. The amending bill and the statute of 1928 itself are designed, first, to protect the buying public in their purchases of articles made of precious metals and, secondly, to protect the dealer and manufacturer. The amendments proposed are minor in character and few in number and should not long detain the attention of the house. The measure itself has been submitted to the manufacturing and retail trades and they have practically unanimously agreed to its terms.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 4 inclusive agreed to.
On section 5-Certificate of master or assayer of royal mint to be evidence of facts stated in certificate.

Has any application ever been made that a referee be allowed under this section? What I mean by referee
is this. Wherever assays are made settling any dispute, it has been the custom to have more than one assayer.

I do not understand that such is the case. I would direct the hon. member's attention to section 18 of the act, which provides in effect that the certificate of the assayer shall be final as a matter of evidence. We must have some way of proving the assay, and in all matters where that sort of thing is done in government offices, where analyses are made, in dealing with that class of evidence or testimony the certificate of the government officer is final and conclusive. I have in mind many of the acts relating to temperance, particularly the old Canada Temperance Act, under which I operated for a great many years, as I have no doubt hon. members who were practising at the bar in the old days also did. You could not proceed otherwise, and it has never been suggested as far as I know that there should be a referee. What is sought here is to meet a difficulty which is arising in connection with the act by reason of court litigation.

What I mean by a referee is this. When disputes arise in connection with assays, even although the assays are made very carefully, many times, when another assayer makes an assay by the same method, it is found that there is a slight difference which is apt to cause trouble. That difficulty is usually met, in settlements in connection with the sale of minerals or metals, by what is known in the mining or metallurgical industry as a referee. I am not suggesting the appointment of a referee, but provision that another assayer may come in.

The matter has not been called to my attention. If that principle is feasible, we have in Ottawa the royal mint and their assay should be final. On the broad principle, I should say that for purposes of prosecution under this act the certificate of the government official should prima facie be final in every case. I do not think there is any reason why we should depart from the practice that has heretofore obtained.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That, it is expedient to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act to facilitate and increase the extension of credit to farmers, to authorize the

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Rhodes
Minister of Finance to purchase additional bonds issued by the board and guaranteed by the government, and to amend the provisions relating to the constitution of the board, the purchase of capital stock, the rate of interest, the amount of outstanding bonds, and supplementary advances.
He said: I am in the hands of the house whether it is preferred that I make a general statement at this stage or we go into committee where there would be a wider opportunity for question and answer in case that might be considered advisable.
May I suggest to the minister that we should like a statement now, not too extensive, but giving us a clear explanation of what is intended by the bill to be founded on the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right. I shall deal only with the general features and the main purposes of the proposed bill, reserving a more detailed discussion to the time when we are in committee on the bill itself.
Perhaps the minister might indicate what changes in interest he has in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall deal with that question as I pass on.
Perhaps the chief purpose of the bill is to do away with the dual control, the divided responsibility and of necessity, of course, the conflict of interests which it has been found in practice has arisen by reason of the fact that we have had provincial boards and the dominion board working under the old arrangement. Under the bill which will be submitted founded upon this resolution, the provincial boards will be abolished and there will be one dominion farm loan board, provision being made for the appointment of a representative of the board in each province. Further, if it is thought desirable, there will be appointed an advisory board to act with him should occasion demand. I may point out in this connection that apart altogether from the difficulties which are bound to arise through the divided authority, the dual control of which I have spoken, the difficulties of the board in its operation have been increased by reason of the fact that the act heretofore has never operated throughout the whole of Canada. For example, it has never operated in Saskatchewan, nor in Ontario, nor in Prince Edward Island, the operation of the dominion act being dependent, according to the terms of the act itself, upon legislation being passed by each province in turn; and as I have indicated, so far at all events the act has not been availed of by the three provinces named.

The board as at present constituted is composed of four members, one of whom is the Minister of Finance who is the chairman. I can not see that any good purpose will be served by discussing the broader question as to the wisdom of a minister of the crown attempting to preside over a board of this character, but I will say this, that with the demands upon the time of the Minister of Finance it is physically impossible for him to attend to the detailed work of presiding at meetings of the board and dealing with individual instances of loans. It simply cannot be done and as a matter of fact, during the whole period of time in which I have had the honour to occupy the office of Minister of Finance, I have been able to attend only one meeting of the board and that was on an occasion of special significance, having to do with the matter of dealing with general, broad principles. So, under the new bill we are proposing that the board shall consist of not less than three nor more than five, the chairman of which shall be the commissioner of farm loans.
Another important provision is enlarging the amount available by way of loans. It will be recalled that under the original Farm Loan Act of 1927 the dominion was authorized to advance a sum only up to 815,000,000, but in the amending act which was passed at the last session we enlarged the amount available to the board in the sum of $40,000,000 by way of advance from the dominion treasury plus an additional $30,000,000 to be made available to the board by means of a dominion guarantee of the bonds of the farm loan board. That provision is not disturbed but we have enlarged the amount in each case by 810,000,000, making a sum of $90,000,000 altogether available for the board.
The proposed bill does away with the provision calling upon the borrower to subscribe to five per cent of farm loan stock and it follows that it should also do away with the necessity for the province subscribing to five per cent of the farm loan stock. Inasmuch as we have encouraged such investments there are contracts outstanding in virtue of which the provinces have subscribed in the aggregate to between $400,000 and 8500,000 of the stock of the board. There is provision in the bill whereby that amount of money be returned to the several provinces that have subscribed.
My hon. friend (Mr. Elliott) has referred to the question of interest. He will recall that in the original set-up of the act it was clearly outlined that the amount of interest to be charged was to be determined by the cost of

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Elliott
money to the board. That principle is not disturbed and it will depend entirely upon the going rates from time to time as to the rate which must be charged tio the individual borrower. While prior to September last I think it was, perhaps a little later, the dominion charged five per cent to the board for money which had been advanced from the federal treasury, that rate was then reduced to four per cent, and I may say, having regard to the then cost of longterm money, because it must be borne in mind that the bonds of the farm loan board are issued for a period of twenty-two years, four per cent was a fair rate. Since that time there has been a lowering of interest rates and while I cannot anticipate the action of the government with respect to a given time or a given rate, it rather looks to me as if it would be possible for the government to lower that rate to three and a half per cent, but I can only announce in a general way that it is the policy and the desire of the government to make available to the farm loan board money as cheap as it can possibly be advanced.
The question of spread between the cost of money to the board and the price at which money is loaned to the individual farmer is of course another matter. I do not know that it would serve any good purpose for me to go into that now other than to say that it is the opinion of the commissioner, Mr. MacLean, and his associates that to keep the board on a fair actuarial basis there should be added to the cost of the money to the board two per cent to cover co^t of administration and a margin of reserve sufficient to build up a fund which could be drawn upon from time to time to absorb the inevitable lasses which occur in making loans. I feel however that that can be reduced, but certainly not below one and a half per cent, because the minimum cost of administration will be one per cent, without any margin of safety whatever. I't may be borne in mind however, that as the sum of loans made increases the board's overhead will be spread over the larger total and therefore the percentage of administration cost will tend to diminish. But in any case, if we are to keep the board in sound financial condition I do not think we can safely go below a margin of one and a half per cent.
There are a number of minor amendments to the act, merely to make it fit in with these broad general principles, but speaking generally I have covered the main alterations and the general principles of the measure.
Will the minister give the names of the members of the board at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The board at present consists of Doctor J. D. MacLean, Mr. Charles Duquette and the Minister of Finance. There is one vacancy.

perhaps I may be pardoned for taking a short time to point out to the minister in charge of the bill and to the Prime Minister and -to the other members of the government who are in the house the immense importance of the subject now under consideration to the farmers of this country. Throughout the country everyone is of one mind in regard to the necessity of making the overhead in the basic industries of production as low as possible. Of these basic industries, all of which are important, I submit that no other is so important as that of agriculture, in which more than fifty per cent of the population of the dominion are engaged. I say to the minister very seriously that while the lot of the farmer has not been easy at any time in the history of this country, it has been much easier at some times than at others. For the past number of years the farmer has been experiencing perhaps the greatest difficulties of anybody engaged in any industry.
I should like to point out something as to the way in which the interest rate has worked in regard to farm loans in, say, the last quarter century. I think I have had fairly wide experience in connection with farm loans. Hon. members will bear in mind that, say, thirty years ago, the loan that was most desired by people who were lending money was what was called a gilt-edged farm loan, one in which the amount loaned was not more than fifty per cent of the actual value of the farm, the value for which it was thought at that time it could be sold at almost any kind of a sale. I recall loans being made to farmers thirty years ago for four and a half and four and three-quarters per cent. Five per cent was quite common. Perhaps the best evidence that could be had of how urgent the present problem is and the great difficulties under which the farmer has been labouring in recent years is the fact that those who were formerly anxious to get farm loans, more anxious, as I say, to get loans on farms than on any other security have practically gone out of the farm loan business in recent years. That has made the position very difficult for the man who has had to borrow money to enable him to carry on his farming business. I submit to the minister that no set of people engaged in any occupation in this country have borne a

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Elliott

heavier share of the burdens of taxation and the other burdens incident to pioneer life in this country than the farmers. I think this is the time when the government should take a very generous view with regard to the rate of interest that should be charged. It is a fact that many of those who are lending money in recent years have felt that it was only the fair thing to do, in view of the low prices the farmer was getting for what he had to sell, to make reductions in the interest and to make substantial reductions in the principal. I think that has been fairly general in regard to farm loans from one end of the country to the other. I might point out that nothing is more to the advantage of the lender than to have a rate of interest which the farmers can pay. A high rate of interest is absolutely impossible in recent years. It is much better to have a rate of four per cent and have the farmer feel he can pay it than to charge five and a half or six per cent, and in some cases higher rates-
Eight per cent.

Yes, but of course eight per cent does not do much good to the lender because he does not get it paid. It is much better to charge four per cent and get it than to charge eight per cent and not get four. That is about the way it works out. The figures the minister has given show that he expects to be able to borrow the money at three and a half per cent. Allowing two per cent for the cost of administration and the losses that must arise in a lending business brings the rate to five and a half per cent, if I understood the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is at two per cent, but it may be one and a half per cent.

Yes, if it should be one and a half per cent the rate will still be five per cent. What I wish to point out to the minister and the government is that at the present time five per cent is altogether out of proportion to the prices the farmer is getting for the product from which he has to pay that interest. I should like to make a few comparisons as to what four per cent means to the farmer to-day with what six and a half per cent meant when this act was first put into force, what five and a half per cent meant later on, and what either five and a half or five per cent would mean to-day. May I direct attention to the following figures, which show the relationship of the prices of farm products and manufactured goods in the years from 1927 to 1934 to the prices in 1926. I point out this fact to the minister and the other members of the government in order to show that for what he buys to-day the farmer pays a much higher rate than he receives for what he has to sell. I point it out also in order to show that to-day four per cent is as high a rate as he can possibly pay. It is equal to a rate of six per cent or six and a half per cent in 1927, judged by what the farmer received at that time.
What is the reason for this situation? I ask hon. members if any one has any doubt at all as to the reason why farmers cannot get loans on their properties to-day except through farm loan boards or organizations of that kind. The reason is not that farmers are less thrifty or less industrious than they were fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years ago. It is that the overhead has become so high and the prices for farm products so low, that it is practically impossible to pay taxes and make ends meet on the ordinary farm to-day, even with the farmer and his family working without wages at all. We talk about minimum wages, unemployment insurance, short hours of labour and all the rest of it. These are all admirable in their own place. No doubt they are necessary in the life of a country developing as Canada is, but I should like to point out that the farmer and his wife and family have no minimum hours of labour or minimum wages. As everyone who knows anything about farm life in this country is aware, they work long hours, depriving themselves of most of the luxuries and many of the absolute necessities of life, and at the end of the year they find themselves in many cases unable to pay their taxes. In other cases they are able to pay part of the interest on the mortgage, but during the last few years it has been very seldom that they have found themselves able to pay any principal.
I am in perhaps as good a position as anyone in this house to know just what difficulties have been encountered by the farmers in the last few years. Those who have not been so enterprising as some of their neighbours have fared perhaps better. The man who in 1925, 1926, 1927 or 1928 had enough faith in himself and in his wife and family to buy

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Elliott
an additional farm and place a mortgage on it, to-day finds himself not only unable to pay any of the principal on that mortgage but has to exert himself to the utmost to pay the taxes on the two farms. In many cases I know of excellent families, descendants of pioneer stock, who for three or four generations have no.t known what it was to be sued, who are being driven off not only the second farm but also off the old home farm because of their inability to keep up payments on the mortgage.
I realize the difficulty in balancing the budget; I realize that this is perhaps the most difficult time we have ever had in Canada in that regard, but I do want to urge upon the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and the other members of the government that something must be done if you wish to keep the people on the farms to-day instead of having them move, as many of them have moved in the last few years after their mortgages have been foreclosed, off the farms into the cities, where they swell the bread lines and increase the number of unemployed. If the people are to be kept on the farms you must bring down the rate of interest to at least four per cent. They cannot pay any more. I do not think that will be denied by anyone who is familiar with farm life. What has taken place in regard to the interest paid on bank deposits? Within the last year the interest on savings bank deposits has been reduced from three per cent to two per cent, a reduction of one-third the former figure or one-half the present amount. The loans that are being floated both by this government and by the Ontario government do not cost nearly as much as they did a few years ago, and of course on short time loans the rate is very much better. I believe that with the utmost care in selecting the persons to whom loans are made the rate can be brought down to the figure I have mentioned. I do not believe any government could grant all the applications that might be made; I think that would be suicidal.
The loans must be kept within reasonable bounds, and the amounts must be such that the farmers can expect to repay, because after all the government do not want a lot of farms on their hands. If they are forced to take over some of these farms they will realize some of the hardships the farms have had to endure in the past few years. I know of one man in a neighbouring county to the one 92582-261
in which I live who was very well off, with a number of mortgages on different farms. I do not know who advised him to do so, but he foreclosed those mortgages when the interest and some of the principal was not paid. As a result that man has had ten or eleven farms on his hands for the last year or two. He was badly enough off before but he is completely bankrupt at the present time. You cannot get anyone to work a farm now at any reasonable rate of rent. As a matter of fact a good many farms throughout the province of Ontario are being rented for taxes at the present time. I expect to have an opportunity later on to say something, but before the bill is introduced I should like to urge upon the minister with all the power at my command, that this matter is most vital to Canada's greatest industry and to the welfare of the Canadian people as a whole. There is not much more that I desire to say now.
We talk about the cost of overhead. No person who knows anything about farming conditions will argue that to-day overhead is not very much greater than it was a few years ago. No one who understands the difficulties with which the farmer who has a mortgage on his farm has to contend will argue that interest is not overhead. Unless we can decrease substantially the overhead to which I have referred we will find many good farms abandoned by some of our very best farmers. That may not be a very bright picture, but it is the truth, and I can see no object ini concealing it.
As I understand the situation the government of the province of Ontario believes that at current borrowing rates they can afford to loan money to the farmers at the rate of four per cent; I hope they can.
During the years to which I have referred I placed loans in the district in which I was practising to the extent of many hundreds of thousands of dollars. Those loans were made on onfy what we call gilt edged security. I believe I reflect the views of the people who loaned the money when I say that during those years even with the low rate of interest a few hundred dollars would pay all the losses that occurred. That has not been the case in recent years.
Perhaps I could not say what I wish to say better than by repeating something I said to the house on a former occasion respecting the plight in which the Canadian farmers now find themselves. Speaking in this house on April 14, 1932. I used words which I believe would apply with equal force to-day and will indicate conditions now existing:

Manitoba, Mr. J. R. McLean of Reston, under date of December 27, 1934. It is as follows:
We have a Federal farm loan board who have not been loaning any money in this territory for some time, although loans have gone through in other districts, and under the new arrangement second mortgages can be secured at low interest rates, for those favoured the last few years with good crops, districts which have been less favored than ours in past years.
I myself have lived in this district for 42 years, having farmed for myself for 31 years. All I own or possess, I have accumulated in 25 years from the farm, the last six years being unprofitable for farmers. I have at least spent $25,000 in improvements, and paid for 2| sections of land as well as $10,000 worth of stock and equipment in the said 25 years, and had clear title to everything previous to the depression. My stock has mostly disappeared by sale for living expenses since.
I made application in 1933 for a loan from the Federal farm loan board and had my farm inspected twice, the last time by the superintendent himself from Winnipeg, J. H. Martinson, and my application has been turned down because of conditions in this locality. This has been done, according to Mr. Martinson, by the head office. This is his assertion, and he goes further to state that he has recommended my application. But I have it on good authority, in fact the best, that the head office has turned down applications from this district which is in your constituency, on the advice of the Manitoba board "which is composed of Mr. Martinson and his two colleagues" and that the head office do not approve of any loans in this district until conditions change.
Now, myself and dozens of others who have still equity in our farm cannot carry on without assistance, and the only assistance I need is a loan to straighten up accumulated debts since the depression, and a nest egg to continue and put in a crop in 1935. I am not going to ask for relief nor accept any, but it seems the first function of a government under the circumstances is to help those who are willing to help themselves, people who have got into difficulty through no fault of their own. I think loans should be made to farmers who have the security to offer, at a low rate of interest, so they can proceed to put in a crop next spring. It is not when seeding starts we need money, but before, so we can he prepared when spring opens up. I hope you will give this matter thought and bring it to the attention of the proper authorities.
After living here for most of my life, and knowing the country with recurring dry years,
I have not lost faith, remembering the great prosperity we enjoyed in years we had sufficient moisture, and it will return.

Jas. R. McLean.
Then, as a typical example, I show hon. members a page from the Country Cuide of its issue of March, 1930. This page shows the place of this farmer, J. R. McLean, and it points to him as an example to the farming community of Canada. It shows his house electrically lighted, his fine class of live stock, and the buildings which Mr. McLean says cost him some $25,000.
(Mr. Willis.]
Now what I desire to point out first is that in a case such as Mr. McLean's apparently neither the Manitoba board nor the federal board take any cognizance whatever of the past record of the farmer. I would point out that the ordinary farm loans are for the period of twenty-three years, not one or two. It seems to me that the Canadian farm loan board should adopt a businesslike basis, or place the prospects of repayment on the basis of the record of the farmer and the record of his land. Rather, it seems that they ask one question and only one: Did you happen to have any rain last year? They ask no questions in regard to the crops he had in 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929. They pay no heed to the fact that during these years the district produced the greatest and the best crops in the province of Manitoba. I submit that the board should follow the ordinary banking practice, which is to investigate the character of the individual and appraise his security and his possibilities of making repayment of the moneys borrowed during the length of the mortgage. At the present time it is undoubtedly true that they are making loans in other parts of Manitoba not nearly as productive over a period of ten years; rather they are making loans where for the last two years they have had some rain, whereas these same districts a few years ago, and for a long period of years, were flooded out by water.
The second point I want to make and the second criticism is that the policy of the Canadian farm loan board is hampering the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act brought forward by the government last year. One of the greatest difficulties in that regard is in connection with rates of interest. If the people in my district could obtain loans at 51 per cent they could, under the machinery of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, obtain a small loan and pay off their creditors, who would be glad to accept cash for maybe 50 or 75 per cent of the amount, and they could start again on the basis of 5| per cent and be very glad to do it. Moreover, it seems to me that the attitude of the Canadian farm loan board is a direct negation of the policy of the federal government. The federal, the provincial and the municipal governments are pouring into that district moneys for the purposes of relief. These governments, in effect, are saying to the people, " We believe you can make a go of it. We believe this is a phase which will pass, this is merely a dry cycle which you have experienced before, and we will help you to carry on." Rut the Canadian farm loan board in its great wisdom comes forward and says, "No. We won't even inspect your

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Willis
farm. We care not whether you have $25,000 worth of buildings and want a loan of only $500 and no more, that has nothing to do with us. We have said it will never rain on your farms again." Remember, the period of the loan is twenty-three years.
In my opinion the attitude of the Canadian farm loan board is entirely incorrect. In Manitoba there are two areas; one is known as drought area A, which is the worst drought area in Manitoba, all unfortunately within my territory, and there is outside that drought area B, not so badly affected. While I have not been able to gather evidence, it seems to me that the attitude of the board is simply this. They say merely, " Oh, you are in drought area B," or whatever it may be. May I say to this house and to the Canadian farm loan board as well that within the so-called drought area B there were this last year crops of 40 bushels of wheat to the acre. It is designated drought area B owing to the fact that the division is by municipalities. Now, the municipalities in western Canada are very large, with the result that you may have complete dryness in the south of the municipality, causing it to be designated drought area B, whereas in another section you may have, as in fact we did have last year, ample crops-good returns to the farmer and apparent prosperity. But they simply say to the farmer that he is in drought area B. As the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) knows, in the municipality of Roblin the southern part may be designated drought area B whereas in the northern part there is apparent prosperity.
The Canadian farm loan board points out correctly that it is not loaning money on compassionate grounds. Certainly it should not loan money on compassionate grounds but should loan on a business basis. May I point out to them however that they can do better from a business point of view by making loans at the present time than they could ten years ago because now a man like McLean, owning two and three-quarter sections of land, with $25,000 worth of buildings would be willing to accept a few thousand and give them a first mortgage, and they would have security which they could not have obtained had they lent the money ten years ago. Further, at the present time within these areas, owing to the fact that in the last couple of years they have had no rain, there is great opportunity for anyone from the standpoint of investing money for the purchase of land, because it can be done so easily. Cash is so important at the present time that they are willing to sacrifice what they have in order to carry on. Therefore greater security can be obtained.
In my opinion, at the present time they are loaning moneys to districts in the northern part of the province which have no past record and no great prospects for the future. But in view of the fact that at present and for a short while they have had some rain there is a willingness to loan moneys there at a time when they could do better, from the point of view of security, by placing loans in other sections of the province.
With the amendments outlined by the minister I am pleased, because I think that the abolition of provincial boards will enable us, if I may say so, to place the blame in the proper quarter. The amount of the advance, $90,000,000, seems adequate. It appears to me however, if we can believe the words of these men, that it may be necessary to have a new personnel in the board in Ottawa, to revamp and reorganize it. It may be necessary to retire some of the members and perhaps the commissioner himself. I say that with all kindness. I do not think that at the time the Canadian farm loan board was set up it was ever contemplated that the present personnel would handle $100,000,000; I do not think it was ever contemplated that the present machinery would do so. I am informed that the commissioner has an appointment dated January 1, 1929, for a period of ten years. In that respect he has his rights which should be safeguarded; he came here on that promise and certainly that should be safeguarded also. But if loans are to be passed by those in Manitoba who have inspected the land and know the situation and are going to be turned down at Ottawa simply because, as they say, the individual is in the drought area, then how can you bring about the change unless you change the personnel of the board? I trust that when the necessary changes are made they will be able to place on the inspection in Manitoba men who have had experience there, who understand where the proper security is and where loans can safely be made, rather than do as they have done in the past. It seems to me that direct federal administration will be an advantage. If the same old attitude is to be adopted as was adopted in the past and loans passed by the inspectors before coming here are to be cancelled and not granted; if the same attitude is going to be adopted in regard to the amounts advanced and the way in which the whole administration is carried out, then it may be necessary, safeguarding the interests of the commissioner in every way, safeguarding his rights, that either he be surrounded with a new personnel or-and I say this in all kindness-the commissioner himself be retired or his attitude changed.

I rise not to be critical of the administration of either the Farm Loan Act or any of the amendments that have been made during recent years in regard to the operation of the act itself, but rather, if I can, to suggest something that may be helpful. In my opinion the situation that to-day affects agriculture from one end of Canada to the other is the most critical in our history. I am simply astounded when I come here and listen to statements made by men coming from what we consider the garden spots of the dominion so far as agriculture is concerned, to learn that competent farmers of many years' experience are finding themselves in serious financial difficulties. I have nothing to say with respect to the administration of the farm loan board or any other board that have loans in the so-called drought areas. I asked a question of a friend of mine: Would you loan money under similar circumstances if it were your own money? When I say that may I say to the minister that the situation in Canada is so critical at the present time that the government in charge and, indeed, the House of Commons should be prepared to take extraordinary chances to save the situation. I for one am prepared to support extraordinary efforts to save a situation of this character. We have been forced to guarantee bonds of railway companies in order to save them and no one knows whether the Canadian people may be called upon to make good in some respects some of those guarantees that we have issued. Our experience in the past has been that even in prosperous times the farm loan business has been a bit precarious from the standpoint of receiving returns expected by those who loaned the money. This cannot be blamed upon the agriculturist. His is a very precarious occupation; he does not know when he makes his investment in labour and money in the planting of a crop whether he is going to reap it or not. I for one have had the experience of beginning to reap a crop and having it all destroyed in a period of a few minutes. That of course is not true of all Canada, but it is just an example of what happens in agricultural pursuits in all parts of this country. So I think we are safe in saying that it is a somewhat precarious undertaking or calling.
I felt the same in 1927 and 1 believe the dominion government in the interest of agriculture, which is so important to the welfare of this country, might by the adoption of a farm loan act be taking some chances on the repayment of the loan. I do not agree with the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) who 
has just taken his seat, that the blame can be laid at the door of the personnel of the board. The Liberal government and this government have surrounded the operations of that board by regulations because it was thought they were warranted. Perhaps they were too onerous, but 1 think if my hon. friend will make inquiry he will find that even in the most prosperous sections in which loans have been made the board has a considerable number of unpaid interest claims. This to me is an indication that despite all the precautions of the board itself and the precautions by the government surrounding the operations of the board, they have not made it immune from the difficulties encountered by others who are lending money under a situation such as this. I make this statement because I do not want to speak in a critical way of either the board or the government itself. Agriculture, in my opinion the most important industry in Canada, is on the verge of bankruptcy and naturally the next thought that occurs to one is: then it must be a very precarious undertaking to loan money to an industry of that character. It is, and I therefore urge the minister and the government that particularly at this time special consideration be given to this matter and, indeed, some chances taken. I believe the government are warranted in taking grave chances, if you will, to save the situation.
As regards Alberta, I am not going to say a single thing about the southern portions of the province; what I have to say and the information I have gathered refers to the northern section where we have never had a crop failure, where eveiy year the farmers have been in receipt of reasonably good returns for their labour in the way of crops. Yet in those favoured localities which are in the constituency which I have had the honour to represent for the last four years-and they are but typical of other sections of the whole of the northern portions of the western provinces-at least 70 per cent of the farmers are facing bankruptcy. That seems a large proportion; nevertheless it is true and seven or eight years ago they were rated among the most prosperous farmers in the country. Conditions however have been such with respect to the price levels that they have been receiving for their produce that they are in that unfortunate position to-day. So bad has it been that the provincial government in their wisdom or otherwise some years ago felt it incumbent upon them to pass what they called a debt adjustment act. It turned out to be nothing more nor less than a debt suspension act and while the creditor could not take

Farm Loan Act-M. Stewart (Edmonton)
action, the unfortunate farmer found himself faced with rapidly increasing responsibilities due to the accumulation of interest and very frequently the accumulation of unpaid taxes. That is the situation which confronts us today. Last year we passed in this house a debt adjustment act and under its provisions we were hopeful that some amelioration could be secured for the farmer. That act has a back-fire that perhaps we did not anticipate in the last session of parliament. The man who is most vitally affected is usually the retail merchant in the locality who has granted credit to these farmers. While his credits may be cut down very materially there is no way for him to secure a reduction of his own indebtedness, incurred largely through giving those credits. I mention that in passing to indicate to the government and the house what a serious situation is developing in Canada in this connection, and how hazardous the tenure of ownership or even tenancy on the farms is becoming. To-day no one is prepared to lend money to an individual engaged in agriculture. That cannot be denied. I have interviewed several mortgage companies and life insurance companies engaged in this business and they say: Not another dollar except to protect the investment we already have; and we would be glad to get our money and get out. That is their attitude. I think the government are to be commended for anything they can do by way of improvement of the act and in securing a larger amount of funds to loan to meet this very serious situation. Last year, in conjunction with the Farmer's Creditors' Arrangement Act, provision was made by amendments to this act that loans could be made for the purpose of tiding the farmer over his serious situation while investigation was being made. I do not know how far that has worked out, I have no information as to how much was done, but judging from what I learned in Alberta very little was done by the farm loan board in the way of loaning last year. I am not going to be critical about that. But the situation in a great many, cases where composition of debts was being sought was that it appeared that while most of the creditors were willing to compromise in a reasonable way on their debts the main difficulty was the mortgage itself, usually held by some corporation. If my information is correct, the corporations holding the mortgages were quite willing to surrender them at some considerable reduction if they were paid off. That would mean of course the transfer of that mortgage to the farm loan board, they being the only agency through which loans might be secured.
But my information is-I cannot say that I know anything personally of this matter- that even with the cutting down by the mortgage companies to a reasonable degree of the principal and accumulated interest as proposed, the amount as so reduced would still exceed the limit of seventy per cent of the present selling value of the land and therefore the farm loan board would be unable to make the loan. I do not blame the farm loan board, but in my opinion we have got to give much more leeway to the board than we have in the past. We have got to modify the regulations. I have never lost a crop on my farms. I had them valued some years ago but if I were asked to-day what they are worth as a productive enterprise I really do not know what I would value them at. And as I say, although we have been frozen, in no year have we lost a crop on those lands and they are typical of a great many others. But if I were sent there as an appraiser to say what the value of a farm is to-day I would have great difficulty. It is all right to talk about the experience of the past, but what is going to be the experience of the future, in the light of what has happened in recent years?
So my whole plea is that a very lenient view be taken of this situation, and that the government take some extraordinary chances in loaning money in order to keep our farmers on the land. The procession of farmers off the land in western Canada, or arrangements with the mortgage companies to farm for the purpose of paying the taxes or on a basis of one-third of the crop, which is the usual rental for farms in that locality, is going on at a tremendous rate. Such a condition breaks the spirit of people who have spent twenty-five or thirty years of their lives trying to build up a competence for themselves and their families. It is useless to go over a recital of what a farmer and his family do in the way of actual labour to secure the returns that they get from a farm even in prosperous years. I do not want to interject a single word that would suggest .that I am blaming the policy of the government for the present situation; I may do that at another time, but this thing is too serious to make a political issue out of it. I shall deal with the policy of the government on another occasion, and perhaps deal as harshly as T can with them in order to see if some amelioration will not be granted in that regard. But I say, speaking for myself, that I am prepared to back the government in taking some very grave chances. I welcome to some degree the suggestion of complete control. A common expres'

sion in western Canada is that there is too much passing the buck when you have the two bodies operating in this connection. As the previous speaker said, agriculture is in perhaps a more difficult situation to-day than it has been for many years, though I do not think it is as difficult as it was two or three years ago. The

hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) suggested that the rate might be lowered to 4 j- per cent; personally I would be glad to see it reduced to 4 per cent but, as hon. members know, the Farm Loan Act provides that the rate must be sufficient to provide for the issue of bonds, the building of reserves, and the expenses of administration. In the province of Ontario I feel that recently the farmers have been in a rather more difficult position with regard to farm loans than has been the case with the farmers of other provinces. In this province we had applications made to the government by over a thousand farmers prior to the last provincial election, to which the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has referred. Of those applicants over five hundred had paid the inspection fee of $12 but, according to my information, not more than fifty applications were accepted. The nature of the mortgage situation in Ontario and the other provinces is very much as the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has stated; the fact that the provinces have issued loans in the past has more or less taken that business out of the realm of private enterprise and, as has been stated, the loaning corporations refuse to lend money, especially if the application has been refused by the province or by the farm loan board. In the province of Ontario, in which as the representative of a riding in that province I am vitally concerned, we have something like $55,000,000 in loans to some 17,000 farmers under the farm loan act of the province. In the past when a farmer needed a loan or desired to buy a farm for himself or his son he naturally thought of getting the money from the farm loan board. That was the custom for many years, but those loans were abruptly discontinued just at a time of crisis, when the need was greatest. During the last session of this parliament the Farm Loan Act was amended to provide that loans might be made not to fifty per cent of the value of the farm but to sixty-six and two-thirds per cent of the value of the farm and chattels, and I believe many provinces have taken advantage of that amendment and have passed enabling legislation.
That amendment was passed in this house in June of 1934, when unfortunately the legislature of the province of Ontario was not sitting. On June 19 an election w'as held; in fact the amendment was passed by this parliament while the election campaign was in full swing. No enabling legislation was passed

in the province of Ontario. The legislature has not met since the election, though we expected a session some time ago as was promised. At any rate the result has been that this enabling legislation has not been passed and relief has been withheld from farmers who are in dire distress, on the verge of going into bankruptcy, and, in some cases subject to the risk of losing the results of twenty-five years of work. He pleaded with the province for a loan, but his application was refused. I understand that the reason given was that the previous government had failed to pass an amendment to the farm loan act, and the board had not the authority to issue the loan. I leave 'that example with this house for what it is worth. Everyone knows that the dominion Farm Loan Act was passed in 1927. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that at the beginning of this session the government have seen fit to step into the breach and bring forward amendments to the act, extending further credit to the farmers of Ontario and of the dominion generally. the lowest possible rate of interest.
