"I would suggest in setting up this scheme that my debt be reduced by 33J per cent and that my interest rate be cut down from its present rate"-which may be 8 or 9 per cent. Hon. members coming from the western provinces are amused when they hear talk about interest rates as low as four per cent, five per cent or even six per cent on mortgages. That does not exist in western Canada. The farmer asks that the interest rate on his debt be cut down to six per cent. Of course the question is,
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Vallance

"What have you to offer?" "Nothing." What is the creditor going to do to me, a farmer, if I come to him and simply suggest that instead of owing him a debt of one hundred cents on the dollar he should accept at some future date seventy-five cents or fifty cents, as has been suggested, and cut the rate down to six per cent. I hope it may be possible under the proposed amendments and through the legislation now contemplated at Regina that the farmer of Saskatchewan may be able to go to the farm loan board and obtain a second mortgage or borrow up to sixty per cent of the value of his land and chattels. If he were able to obtain $1,000 or $1,500 or whatever amount the board saw fit to extend to him he could then approach his creditors and possibly make some adjustment. We find that in the province of Saskatchewan there are very few if any adjustments being made simply through lack of funds to make them. Representing a rural constituency in the province of Saskatchewan I feel that I may endorse all that has been said by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). As an individual from Saskatchewan I am prepared to give every assistance to the government in passing the legislation if such legislation is as outlined in the resolution.
Dealing with conditions in Manitoba the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) directed his remarks to the dried out area. I cannot understand why the farmers in those dried out areas have found it difficult to obtain loans simply because of the fact that over a certain period of time the precipitation has been such and such or so and so. I should like to observe however than when we take a specific period of time between two points, periods of five or ten years, and leaving out the last four or five dry years, we find that the production in that portion of Saskatchewan now known as the dried out area was greater by volume and value than that of the northern areas. All the southern portions need is rain. I know rain cannot be given to them under the Farm Loan Act, but I do believe the act could help the farmers to carry on until such time as they do have rain. It is utterly impossible in many portions of western Canada, and more especially in the dried out areas, for farmers to borrow money, even on mortgages. Going through the country I had farmers tell me that the mortgage companies are not bothering them, the machine companies are not bothering them, and the banks are not bothering them. Why not? Because there is nothing to take. I say that if the farmers of Saskatchewan are contemplating an adjustment of debt now is 
the time to do it. If Saskatchewan's dried out area ever gets a crop, just watch the mortgage companies, the banks and the machine companies. If those dried out areas, over a period of years, can get back to their former average of production the banks, mortgage companies and machine companies will climb on to the farmers and make it utterly impossible for them to carry on. To-day the farmers are not being bothered, and my suggestion would be that they should get an adjustment of their debts. I think that would be possible. If with the $90,000,000 now at its disposal the board would advance credits to the farmers it would confer a great blessing not only on the dried out areas in Saskatchewan but on the western provinces generally.
My farm is located between the dried out areas and the northern areas. As the hon. member for Souris has said, one-half of the municipality might be said to be in the dried out area because, strange as it may seem, we find the dried out areas are slowly creeping north, annually. We find the grasshopper plague is doing the same thing. In my constituency we hope we will not have in the coming season a grasshopper plague such as we have had in the last two years. I have been in the one community for twenty-eight years, and only in the last two years have we experienced a total crop failure. I feel sure that when the farmers in the west, and particularly those in the province of Saskatchewan, read in the newspapers that the federal Farm Loan Act is to become operative, and that there is $90,000,000 to loan to the farmers, they will be greatly pleased. I hope the board will not deal too strictly with those portions of Canada which have not been so favoured climatically as many others.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations concerning this resolution. Not from a political standpoint, and in all seriousness I want to say that never was there a more cruel decision made than the decision of the authorities in the province of Ontario to discontinue the operation of the Ontario development board. The hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) has said that thirty years ago farm mortgages were a gilt edged investment. As compared with other investments I would say the same is true to-day. I believe if an analysis were made of losses on investments we would find that the percentage of losses on farm mortgages in eastern Canada is very much lower than on other kinds of investments. The same was true, so far as ithe Ontario development board was

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Porteous
concerned. I had considerable experience in negotiating between that board and some of the applicants, and my experience was that upon some occasions the board were not lenient enough. They said they would not take mortgages over fifty per cent of the value of the farm. If that was not a gilt edged investment I do not know what could be.
A good many angles to this problem have been presented this afternoon. One was that we should have a lower rate of interest, especially in the province of Ontario, and with that I agree. Another hon. member believed there was not sufficient credit extended to the farmers at any rate of interest. I believe both those points may be well taken. I agreed further with the hon. member for Souris in his observations concerning .the dried out areas. In my view credit extended to the people in those sections of the country where crops are uncertain should be based on a long period, and not a short period of only two or three years. It should be on a long term basis for a period of possibly twenty years, and both from a business and actuarial standpoint the rate should be as low as possible; but, Mr. Speaker, it should be at cost. The farmer as yet is not a charity patient. If you were to base the rate of interest upon his ability to pay, then in some cases, judging by the last few years, the farmer would not pay any interest at all, but the farmers are not asking for .that sort of thing because it is charity. I believe that the farmers in some cases have been asked to carry burdens unjustly, 'but nevertheless they are not going to ask for charity.
The rate of interest should be as low as possible on a business like basis of course, and it should be at cost. That is all the farmers are asking. The cost also should be kept as low as possible. I think myself that a spread of li per cent is possibly too much. I think that with a fair administration of this program there would be very few losses, and I think there would be no losses at all if it is administered properly, in which case the spread could be less than li per cent. I also think that in the near future money will be borrowed more cheaply, and the rate of interest could be arranged so that it would be lower to the farmer than is anticipated at the present time.
I want to make just one more suggestion, and that is that in setting up the machinery to administer this act as amended, the minister should take into consideration the possibility of associating it with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I think before
long, if we have not got them right now, we shall have some most enlightened receivers so far as the farmers' ability to pay is concerned under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and I think that the advice of those receivers might be a great advantage to the board that might be set up, and I should like to see these two activities associated and carried on together.
As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and some other hon. gentlemen have said, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is now operative, but it does not go far enough, and if there was some credit available so that those people who have burdens of debt could receive credit, many of them would take fifty or sixty per cent of their debt and make a settlement.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up very much of the time of the house on this question of amending the Canadian Farm Loan Act, but I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to what I consider is one of the causes why the interest rate is so high, and perhaps it is also one of the reasons why the minister feels that the rate could not be lowered to the point that has been suggested during the discussion this afternoon.
I have had something to do with helping farmers to obtain loans under this act, and I find that the cost is extremely high. Take a farmer needing a loan of $1,000, for instance. He cannot get that loan under a cost of $50. First he has to send in $10 for an appraisal. Then an appraiser is sent out, and when his appraisal is in and the board is considering the proposition of making a loan to the farmer, he is instructed by the local board that he must be prepared to pay $35 or $40 more when the time comes to search the title and make out the mortgage.
Let me give a case in point. An application for a loan of $1,000 was made through the local board in New Brunswick. First we had to send $10 for an appraisal. The appraiser lives within half a mile of the man who was making application for the loan. There was $10, and all the work that that appraiser had to do could be done within three or four hours. The application is considered favourably. In the application you have to give a description of the property as it is on record. The lawyer or the legal firm to whom instructions are given to make out the papers have not much searching of records to do because the whole thing is there before them, and yet it costs the farmer $35 or $40.
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Verdot

Now such costly proceedings must add considerably to the overhead, but if you cut down that overhead, and I believe it could be cut down by 50 per cent on every application, you could also cut down the cost of administration, and that perhaps would give you the opportunity of loaning the money at a lower rate of interest.
I was pleased to hear the minister state that the local boards will be abolished. I understand by that, that the work will be done entirely from Ottawa, with the assistance perhaps of agents in the field. Let me draw the minister's attention to the fact that that will mean a considerable reduction in the overhead if the work is properly looked after. That is another source of reduction in overhead which may make possible the loaning of the money at the rate suggested in the discussion this afternoon.
But I should like to urge on the minister this point: For gracious sake, in naming appraisers, do not have it done in the way it is being done now by the local boards. Why, Mr. Speaker, the appraisers that are named in the province of New Brunswick have no more idea of valuing properties than I have an idea of clinching the moon with my teeth. I know it. I am interested myself, and have been for years, in the valuation of property, as chairman of boards of assessors and as chairman of school district boards, where the chairman and the secretary together have experience in the valuing of properties.
There is another point, although this may not be repeated under the amendment to the act, but in the past when times were very good, appraisers have been named who were interested themselves in loaning money to farmers, and when they went to appraise the property, they simply sent in such a report that the farmer could not get a recommendation from the local board for a loan. The local board was blamed for that, and the head office at Ottawa was blamed for it when it should fltit have been blamed except for naming such an appraiser. That appraiser, after seeing that he had knocked out the chances of the farmer for getting a loan under the board, would then come forward himself and lend the money. I know cases of that kind, and that is one reason why I am pleased to see that the local board is to be abolished and that the head office here at Ottawa will have charge of the administration of the act.
I feel sure that it will result in more efficient administration, with greater satisfaction to the farmer.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it is a pleasure for me to endorse this resolution and to see such unanimity upon it. It seems that we are agreed one hundred per cent on the resolution, and I know it will be gratifying to the farmers of western Canada as well as to those of the east to know that the sum of 890,000,000 is to be devoted to the purpose the government has in view. Hon. gentlemen who have already spoken have indicated the difficulties which confront the farmers of the west, but I would point out that there are still a good many farmers who have not been forced to put on a first mortgage. The question therefore is, what about those who have not yet had to go to a mortgage company for assistance? Can they get any benefit through the farm loan board? So far as I have been able to ascertain, it would appear that there is a possibility for such farmers to get some assistance.
One important question, a question on which I feel very strongly, is that of interest. It has been my privilege in the last few months to see many applications favourably received for the writing down of debts owed by farmers. There is no question whatever about it that interest is a millstone around the farmer's neck, at any rate in western Canada. The debt is very often doubled as the result of interest. Take a mortgage of 85,000; in the last four or five years the debt has almost doubled. The average rate is eight per cent and when you compound the interest you can see how onerous the burden becomes.
As regards the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, we are getting results. I have been receiving letters from farmers in my constituency in which they express their appreciation of the writing down of their debts. In other words, there seems to be cooperation . between the creditors and the farmers; there may be a few instances in which this is not true, but generally speaking it is. The other day I received a letter from a farmer who lives not very far from me. He is a man of about seventy. He told me that he had taken new heart and courage and he complimented the receiver in my town on the way in which he had made it possible for this farmer to have his debts written down. Previously, he said, he had been disheartened; he had given up hope; but now he feels that it is possible for him to meet his obligations, in part at any rate.
There is however a difficulty in connection with the unsecured merchants throughout the

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Loucks
little towns. Most of them would be glad to-day to take fifty per cent of what is outstanding in their accounts. That is the information I have received from most of the merchants in my district, but when they are asked to write down debts, however willing they may be to do this, there is no money forthcoming to enable them to finance their business. They are still obligated to the wholesalers one hundred per cent. They say that if it were possible for them to get fifty cents on the dollar from their debtors they could carry on. With that money they could go to the wholesaler and come to some arrangement with him, but it does not avail them anything to write down debts fifty per cent and receive no money at all.
In my part of the country I do not know how they are going to put in a crop this spring if they have no money, and most of the farmers have not a dollar. During the last three or four years the deterioration in machinery has been something terrible, and the trouble has been aggravated by the dryness, because the land is so dusty that the machinery deteriorates much more quickly than it would ordinarily. But I have not given up hope, Mr. Speaker. There is a future before us. I have lived in that part of the country for thirty years and until a few years ago I never had a complete failure, though I have experienced two now.
About the first of November I had occasion to visit the dried out area in my constituency, a district about seventy-five miles from where I live, where they have had four complete failures. In this district there are mostly Finlanders, and I attended a meeting of the ratepayers' organization, comprising some two hundred of these people. When they got to the meeting these farmers were apparently so discouraged that they almost felt like hanging the reeve of the municipality, whom they blamed for the plight in which they found themselves.
A member of parliament?

No, he was not a member of parliament. I was told that if I got on the platform something might happen to me, but I did. I told the chairman of this organization that I was not afraid to face my audience and so I got on the platform and spoke to these men-there were women also -for three-quarters of an hour, and then I suggested to the chairman that he should throw the meeting open for a sort of fellowship meeting. He did so, and I should like to give you the testimony of some of these
people, not all Finlanders. One man said, "I went through the great war, fighting from the beginning to the end. To-day I have a family of seven. This morning I took five of these children to school without any shoes on their feet, though it is the first of November. But I am determined to keep my children at school as long as I can." There was condemnation, not of this government but of the provincial authorities, on the ground that all they were allowing these people was $5 for adults for clothing. This man said it would not buy a pair of boots, and yet he had seen billions of dollars blown away in the great war. He said he had put in his crop the last year in the hope that there would be a harvest, and there he was, unable to get enough money to buy boots for his children. But what encouraged me, Mr. Speaker, at this meeting of two hundred ratepayers, was the optimistic spirit of the farmers after all that they had come through. They said that if it were possible for them to obtain a little bit of money to carry them along they were quite willing to continue.
When we reflect that a few years ago that country produced great crops, we cannot think that there is no future ahead of us. Indeed, the possibilities in Saskatchewan may be beyond the comprehension of some eastern people. We have excellent soil there; some of the best of it lies in that dry area. Would it be advisable therefore for these people to move to the western states, when we know that the same condition prevails right down to the gulf of Mexico?
I am glad that the Minister of Finance is taking steps to help the farmers out of their difficulties, making it possible for them to pay back the money in the future. But as I said before, I feel very strongly on the question of interest, which in my opinion should not be more than four per cent. When we take into consideration the overhead and administration of some of these mortgage companies, I think we are justified in the contention that interest should not be higher than that rate. In our section of the country many of the farmers are to-day assigning a third crop to the mortgage companies. Let me point out what happens in connection with those mortgages. An agent comes out and drives all over the farm to see how the crops are coming along and all this overhead is charged to the farmers in my section. There is no necessity for this because a crop survey is made every year. It is clear that a great deal of this overhead can be eliminated .
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Loucks

Further, the dominion government, if we are going to get lower rates, must set the example. There is no use in going to the mortgage or insurance companies to endeavour to get them to charge a lower rate. If the government cannot get cheap money for us it is hopeless to expect to get it from the mortgage and insurance companies. Just a few days before I came to Ottawa I visited the court of review in Saskatoon and I met the manager of the Toronto General Trusts Corporation. He knows me well. He said to me: " Look here, Bill, the government has not gone far enough yet. Do not forget this: we who represent the trust company are obligated for a great amount of money over in Great Britain; we are obligated also to insurance companies at a certain rate around five or five and a half per cent. The government of Canada should go to the fountain head, to those who loaned us the money, and see if something cannot be done by them to bring the rates down; then it will be possible for us and the other companies to meet the request of you farmers." In other words, he said: We are still obligated for five or five and a half per cent interest to big financial firms in Great Britain and even to insurance companies, some of them in this country, who have loaned us a great deal of money, so you see the necessity of the government going to the fountain head to find out if something cannot be done. While I have great sympathy for widows and orphans, I do not believe at the present time there is much money invested by the widows and the small investors; I think most of this money that is being administered through the mortgage companies is coming from big financial concerns. When I think of the farmers who went from eastern to western Canada, many of them from Ontario-and I am one of them-who took the risk and went out to the west as they did, investing there what they had, and who made good and made that country one worth while to live in, every consideration should be given by this government to those people so as to retain them on the land, looking forward to the time when conditions will improve.
The hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol) suggests that I should give the house some information as to what we have accomplished in that western country. The amount of wealth we have produced is too great to be realized, but billions and billions of dollars' worth of wheat have been taken out of western Canada. When I think of my own little town of Delisle shipping
[ Mr. Loucks r
over a million bushels of wheat in 1915, Rosetown shipping over a million bushels, and similarly with different towns all along the line-that was when wheat was at a much higher price than it is to-day-I think I am safe in saying that money has come from western Canada to the east in billions. One unfortunate circumstance affecting the people out there is that when the price of wheat went down so low the price of the things they consume did not fall commensurately, and that was pretty hard on the farmers.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. gentlemen for allowing me to say a few words in regard to this resolution. I rise with a good deal of trepidation, this being my maiden speech in this chamber. I have listened with much interest to this debate, expecting that it would take on the aspect of a discussion of a resolution regarding a federal farm loan act, but I note that a good deal of it has been concerned with what has happened in Ontario in regard to the agricultural development board.

Farm. Loan Act-Mr. Campbell
Just in passing, before I speak directly to the resolution, it is only fair that I should say something respecting the working of that board during the last five or six months or a little longer. It is very true, as the hon. member for Dufferin^Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Por-teous) have said, that during last summer and up to the present time many people in Ontario have been looking for loans. It is also true that a good many applications were received by the board prior to the election held on June 19 last, and that many of those applications were approved just prior to that election, and that some of them have not been approved by the board to the extent that a loan has been made. I want to make it clear to all hon. members that prior to the month of May the interest rate on farm loan mortgages in Ontario stood at six per cent. During the provincial election campaign, in which I had the privilege of taking an active interest, it was announced that that rate would be lowered to five and a half per cent and, as has been stated by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), it was cut to five per cent during the heat of the election. The people throughout the province did not really know just what was happening. When the new provincial government took office they made an investigation to find out just how the agricultural development board stood, and they discovered that some $55,000,000 of the people's money had been loaned throughout Ontario. One unfortunate experience was that many loans had been made, not for the purpose of allowing a farmer to permit his son to purchase a farm and some *new stock and start up in business, or for the farmer to improve his farm by building a new bam or house, but rather at the instance of influential people, supporters of the late government, and the fact is that they wanted to turn to the agricultural development board many mortgages which were due and on which the interest was very much past due. That is a serious statement to make, but it is a fact that has been ascertained. Other instances were found in which the board had neglected their business to such an extent that the new board found themselves the owners of many farms on which taxes had not been paid for two or three years. In the township south of the one in which I happen to live, the agricultural development board now has on its hands four farms, on two of which there was no tenant and the taxes had not been paid for over two years; and in one instance the farm was advertised for taxes last fall and redeemed by the board. When 92582-27
the new board made a survey they found that if this $55,000,000 odd of loans were liquidated the province of Ontario would suffer a great loss. Therefore they reorganized the board, made further investigation, and it was decided to carry on. They are trying to sell many of these farms, and the province of Ontario will, no doubt, not suffer as great a loss as at first seemed possible.
The statement was made this afternoon that no loans have 'been made by that board. I happen to know that during the months of November and December some seventy-two loans were made, amounting to something like $140,000, or an average of about $2,000 each. These loans were made to people who wanted to purchase stock or improve their buildings, or who had sons that they wanted to start on farms for themselves-the purpose for which the board was originally started. It was announced by the present federal government just after the election that the farm loan board and the Farmers Creditors' Arrangement Act would be in operation in the near future, and it was intimated that the interest rate charged would be somewhat lower than was current in Ontario. Consequently I have no doubt received as many applications as the hon. member for North Grey or the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. Many of these people have withdrawn their applications from the provincial authorities, or the agricultural development board of Ontario, waiting to see what is going to happen in the working out of this farm loan act. It was also announced by the Ontario agricultural development board some time ago that the interest rate there would be only four per cent. That was to come about because they said they would be willing to pay the difference between what the federal farm loan board would charge for the money loaned under this act and the four per cent. I note however that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) said to-day that that arrangement would not be allowed to be carried out. Therefore the farmers of Ontario are to be deprived of the chance of receiving money at four per cent, unless the government will consider lowering the interest rate to that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me, I regret to have to interrupt; it is quite contrary to my custom, but he is under an entire misapprehension in saying that the minister said that any action of this government will prevent the people of the province of Ontario from receiving money at four per cent.



Farm Loan Act-Mr. Campbell

I did not mean just what I think the minister understood me to mean. I merely state that the province of Ontario announced through the Minister of Agriculture that money would be made available on farm mortgages at four per cent. The plan would be that the money would be borrowed from the federal farm loan board, and if the interest rate were higher than four per cent the provincial government would for the benefit of the farmers pay the difference between the four per cent collected from the farmers and the rate paid to the farm loan board. I mention that, as I understand from what has been said to-day that the farm loan board is going to operate as a federal body and that the provincial boards will have nothing to do with it. By that action the people of Ontario will be prevented from receiving that benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that happens it will be the fault of the provincial government, not of this government.

No; I want to go a little further. The Minister of Finance and his government still have a chance to give to the people of Ontario that benefit by a reduction of interest rates to four per cent. This is a vital point that I want to make clear. Notwithstanding the claims made by the hon. members from western Canada I represent probably the most agricultural riding in the dominion; there is only one incorporated village in my riding, and that has only seven hundred people. The people in my riding are farmers, with a few miners and lumbermen. They represent probably the most substantial class of citizens that this province is privileged to have. They are all descendants of United Empire Loyalists; they have resided there for many years; the farms are mostly owned by their occupants and have been in the family for generations. The only sales made are probably from one family to another as a farmer wants to get a farm for his son. Unfortunately during the last two or three years, on account of falling revenues, the father is not helping the son out, and consequently we have in the counties of Frontenac and Lennox and Addington a large number of farms for sale, and a large number of farm boys for whom farms cannot be bought on account of the interest rates that would have to be paid on a mortgage; consequently they are just staying home and living off the parents. If the Minister of Finance would study the amount of production from the

agricultural industry for the last five years ne would find that it is impossible for anyone connected with that industry to pay more than three per cent. I have no doubt that even though interest rates should be down to four per cent many mortgages will be in ai'rears for interest, on account of local conditions, sickness or otherwise. But the government must take cognizance of the fact that the farming and agricultural industry needs just as much help as do the labouring people who by reason of the present tariff and other policies of this government find themselves out of employment.
This morning I received two letters from constituents saying that the mortgages on their farms are held by estates-two different estates, I may add; there is no connection between the two, because the farms are in different townships. It is necessary that both estates be wound up in the near future. In both cases the lawyers find there is no money available to have someone else take over the mortgage, at any interest rate. Probably there are many cases of this kind throughout the whole dominion. Either the farmer must lose the farm through foreclosure or the estate must take less money for a quick settlement. If the government could see its way clear to allowing money to be loaned at a reasonable rate of interest, it would be a very great advantage to the farmers and also to people holding mortgages in cases such as I have just mentioned. I am not going to say what the rate should be; I do not wish to take up too much time, but the fact is that unless you lower the interest rate to around four per cent either this government or the government to follow will have a very sad experience in connection with tfie collection of interest and principal.
I want to point out something further. All during my recent election campaign the question of lower interest rates, not only on farm mortgages but on government loans and so on, was debated at great length. I was criticized by some hon. gentlemen opposite for the statements I made, but I want to point out that the people of Frontenac-Addington, composed mainly of agriculturists and who realize the severe burden they are bearing at the present time, by electing me have asked this government to reduce interest rates to the greatest extent possible.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a very few remarks to what has been said already in connection with this measure. I do not think the govern-

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Gobeil
ment can be too highly praised for the amendments proposed. There are several reasons why I make that statement, some of which have been stated already.
The first change suggested is the elimination of the provincial boards, and I am very glad to be able to say that I find myself in perfect accord with some hon. members opposite, especially the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), in their expressions of opinion as to this move. By the way, I should like to remark that for the last week or ten days we have been witnessing quite a strange scene. Since the house opened we have been told by some hon. members opposite that the radio speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) were delivered only for the purpose of getting votes; one hon. member went so far as to call them bluff. But when these reform measures are brought down, what do we see? Even hon. members opposite are very anxious to rise and place themselves on record as approving them.
Before I digressed, Mr. Speaker, I was saying that I find myself in accord with the hon. member for Gloucester with regard to the provincial boards. I do not wish to say anything in a political way in regard to those boards, because I do not believe in giving the last blow to a dying man, and if my judgment is correct these boards are on the eve of passing away. But at least this will clear up the situation. Certainly I have had more correspondence in regard to farm loans than in regard to anything else during the past four years. Sometimes I have had to write three or four letters to the same man, all because responsibility could not be placed. I do not wish to say anything harsh with regard to the inspectors or even the members of the provincial boards, but the personnel of the boards was submitted by the different provincial governments, and it goes without saying that most of those appointed-and in the case of our province I think I can say all those appointed-were of the same political faith as the provincial government. So it was only to be expected that even if there was no partiality the people whose applications were refused would think this had been done in many cases because of their political faith. I do not suggest that all who apply for loans in future will get them, but at least they will know who refuses the loan. They will not be told by one person that their loan was refused by the provincial board and by another that the loan was refused by the federal government. That is one desirable feature of the suggested amendments.
92582-27J
Another improvement I wish to commend is the fact that in future borrowers will not have to contribute five per cent of the loan. This was another bad feature of the act, and the borrowers could not understand why they should be borrowers and lenders at the same time. Many times a farmer who needed $1,000 foimd that, in addition to what it might cost him for a clear title, he received only $950 instead of $1,000, because he had to subscribe five per cent of the loan.
The resolution does not say that is to be changed.

I understood the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to make that statement.
I also wish to join with the hon. member for Gloucester as to the matter of titles. Probably the government cannot help themselves-
Yes, they can; let the government fix a fee.

That might be done. I should like to point out that in the province of Quebec the situation is worse than it is in other provinces. I could mention two cases, in my own parish. One man borrowed $1,500, and the cost of securing a clear title was $149. So, with the five per cent that he had to subscribe to the board, instead of receiving $1,500 he received not quite $1,300. I know of many other cases where the cost was well over $100.
I had a note before me in connection with appraisers, a point mentioned by the hon. member for Gloucester. I do not believe it is necessary to go into the matter in detail, but I may say that I agree with him. If I were to suggest anything to the government A would be that they should choose appraisers carefully. I make the suggestion without any thought of criticism. Although in the province of Quebec we have had some very worthy appraisers, on the other hand some had no experience in farm values and a few were nothing more or less than political appointees. It may be that most new appraisers named by this government would be Conservatives-I hope most of them would be-but I would find no fault if some were Liberals. First of all, I would say, "Get a good man, a man with experience who knows the values of farm properties and who could do justice not only to the government but to the borrower."
I believe I have nothing further to say on the resolution, although I may make some1

additional observations when the bill is before the house. For the time being I shall conclude by saying that I heartily endorse the principle embodied in the resolution.
Mr. G. G. COOTE Macleod):	Mr. Speaker, so much has been said in regard to the resolution that I have only one or two observations to make. I feel that there are two points which should be emphasized even to a greater extent. The first is that the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act were what might be termed companion bills. I think one hon. member said they were twins. I believe the two acts should be taken together when we are dealing with the farm debt and farm credit situation. I have discussed the matter with men who have been actively connected with the administration of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and it is only because of representations made to me by them that I now speak.
The greatest difficulty farmers find to-day in making arrangements with their creditors under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is that there are mo credit facilities available to them. Many of these men who wish to make arrangements with their creditors could do so on favourable terms, if they could get the cash to turn over in settlement of whatever percentage of their liabilities is agreed upon. A great many men could obtain a fifty per cent reduction of their liabilities if they could get a loan for that amount. Of course that is if the whole proceeds could be turned over to their creditors. It seems to me that if in many cases the farm loan board were given instructions by the government, instructions which I think the government should take the responsibility of giving, loans could be made. In other words, I wish to agree with what was said so well by the, hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). In my view the time has come when in the national interest as well as in the interest of agriculture the government should show their willingness to assume some of the risk entailed in granting loans. I believe they should Say frankly to the men administering the farm loan act, "We anticipate you will have some losses, and we do not think it necessary that all the losses you incur in making loans in these times must be charged up to the operation of the act and included in the interest you are going to endeavour to collect from the people to whom you make loans." It would be far better for the board and for the government to have loans under the farm 
loan act in respect of which they would have a reasonable expectation of collecting the interest named on the face of the mortgage, because once a large number of borrowers get in arrears and find they cannot pay there seems to be a temptation for those who perhaps, by struggling hard enough, could pay, to allow their interest payments to stand.
I would have a great deal of sympathy with any person administering the farm loan board to-day. I do not mean to say that I excuse all the decisions the board has made in the past, but unless they have some specal instructions from the government, or provisions in the act to warrant their running risks, they will not take them. They know perfectly well that the present level of farm prices is such that in many cases the loans being applied for are too large. That is, the earning capacity of the farmer, due to present price levels, is not sufficient to pay the interest. Those in charge of farm loans do not like to have loans placed on their books which they have no good reason to believe will be kept in good standing. There is no guarantee given to the farm loan board that price levels will be raised. We know that at the present time there is a slight raise in price levels.	I have before me the last
monthly statement of the Bank of Nova Scotia in which are set out farm revenues in the Dominion of Canada for the past three years. I have worked out the figures on a per farm basis, and without going into detail may I say that the average farm income in 1928 was approximately SI,600. In 1932 it had fallen to $630, in 1933 to $600, and in 1934 had raised slightly to $745. There has been a slight increase, but not sufficient to enable the farmer to pay any interest, if he is giving his family a decent standard of living. Any hon. member could easily demonstrate that it was easier for a farmer to pay eight per cent in 1926 than to pay anything to-day. As a matter of fact interest can come only out of farmers' surpluses. It can come out of the revenue available after his living and his necessary expenditures have been deducted, and we know that for the last three or four years there has been no such surplus. If the farmer has paid any interest at all he has paid it because of a reduced standard of living or from capital savings. He may have used his insurance savings. The difference between $1,600 in 1928 and $600 in 1933 has taken away the farmers' ability to pay taxes, to pay interest, to buy new machinery, to pay insurance premiums and to provide for the health and education of his family.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had been emphasizing that in my opinion it is necessary that greater facilities be provided under the Farm Loan Act if the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is to effect anything like the purpose for which it was intended. I simply want to say in that connection that I think the rate of interest should not be more than four per cent, and if these greater facilities are to be provided at a rate which agriculture can pay, it is quite clear that the government must be prepared to assume some liability, at least enough to take care of that part of the rate of interest which has always been added in order to cover the risk of loss. I am not going to labour the point any further because I think it has been emphasized several times this afternoon, so that the minister must surely be convinced by now that this is really necessary.
I have had several cases brought to my attention of men who have been endeavouring to get loans, and who have not found it necessary to make any arrangement with their creditors under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I shall mention only one which I think is typical of a good many others. This farmer has a small farm of 160 acres, sixty acres of which is broken. He has I think fifty head of cattle. He is trying to get a small loan to enable him to put up some better buildings, particularly a dairy bam, but so far he has been unable to interest the board even to the point of encouraging him to send in the $10 to cover the inspection fee. It may be that the board in their wisdom feel that they cannot make that loan, but it does seem to me that we must have some better credit facilities for agriculture that will enable a man in that position to get a small loan in order to put him in a position where he can produce under more favourable conditions. I have seen enough correspondence to convince me that a more liberal loan policy must be adopted on the part of the officials in charge of the board if the Farm Loan Act is to meet in any way the present needs of agriculture in the matter of credit facilities.
Without taking up any further time of the house I would again urge on the minister that the government, in whatever legislation they bring down, provide in it or decide as a matter of government policy that the government itself will assume some of the risk in connection with the losses that will be made from now on.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer a few suggestions to the minister and the house based on the conditions that I have found prevailing in the riding that I have the honour to represent. During the last three or four years I have had occasion to come in contact with farmers' indebtedness to a very large degree, and the conditions I have found are these-and incidentally may I say that I do not think anybody can discuss this resolution without linking it up with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
In my riding the average farm consists of 240 to 320 acres. We will take, for the sake of argument, a farm of 320 acres. Say that a man owes $8,000 on a half section of land. If he is able to take advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and get his indebtedness reduced, say, fifty per cent, that still leaves him with an indebtedness of $4,000. Now if this resolution and the bill to be founded upon it will take care of such a case and allow a man who has had his indebtedness reduced say forty or fifty per cent to consolidate his remaining indebtedness in one loan spread over a period of years, twenty or twenty-two years I think the act says, and only very small annual payments are provided for, he might be able to get out from under. But unless the Farm Loan Act and the regulations that will govern its administration are able to take care of that situation I doubt very much if we are going to make much headway in the readjustment of farmers' indebtedness. In the last few years I have found that many creditors were willing to make readjustments, but they all asked the farmer: What consideration will the loan company get if I reduce your indebtedness? The farmer finds himself in a position where he is unable to say to the loan company or to any of his creditors: I will give you your cash if you will reduce my indebtedness.
I do not think there is any great demand in the country for new loans. Of course there might be in certain districts where people want to get a start, but in my opinion the great demand is to relieve the farmer of the indebtedness which he incurred during the period of high commodity prices, and unless this act takes care of that situation so that the farmer after he has had his debt readjusted will be able to consolidate his remaining indebtedness in one loan, I doubt very much whether this legislation is going to be a success.
May I make these few observations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes)-and I do not do it at all in any way of criticism

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Beaubien
[DOT]of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which was passed last summer. Probably it took a little time to get the act under way. As far as I can find out, in the province of Manitoba the board of review has not as yet given any decisions to speak of; if so, it must have been very recently. I find this fear existing, that the farmer was not sure whether the board of review had the right to force a secured creditor to readjust the farmer's indebtedness. In fact I took this matter up with several legal minds in the city of Winnipeg, and I have not yet been able to get a clear and definite understanding whether the board of review has or has not the right to say to the secured creditor who has, say, a first mortgage on the farm: You will have to take so much, and the readjustment will be based on the value that you voluntarily put on the productivity of the farm, or that the board of review puts on it.
When the provincial boards are abolished I assume a provincial representative will have to be appointed for each province. I trust that these representatives and the board here in Ottawa will make every effort to relieve the farmer who is indebted to such an extent that he will never get out from under unless he is able to readjust his debt under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and I would urge that the board be not too critical of the loans after the man's whole indebtedness has been reviewed by the receivers and the board of review under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. If this legislation, with the increased credit facilities that are to be placed at the disposal of the board, is administered as it should be, and if due consideration is given to the ability of the farmer under present conditions to pay and to the capacity of his land to produce enough to pay at present prices, some good might be accomplished. But even when you have reduced your debt by say fifty per cent, calculate on the basis, not of 18,500 but of $4,000, at 51 per cent, and you have $220; and then you have to figure on your municipal and school taxes, at least fifty cents an acre. You must also take into consideration repairs and upkeep of buildings, which would not be less than $100 a year. Then there are other incidental expenses which would add to your overhead, to say nothing of the cost of seeding and of harvesting your crops, and many other costs which enter into farming. So that when you take all these things into consideration the farmer will still find it very 
difficult to make both ends meet. It is therefore only by amortizing his indebtedness, consolidating it under one head and making small annual payments, the rate of interest being reasonably low, that he can clear his home from indebtedness.
I offer these suggestions in the hope that they will be considered. Very often we feel that the officials are not administering the act as we should like them to, but the difficulties are numerous and they do the best they can. At the same time I think the government should instruct the boards which will administer the act to carry out its provisions having in mind present commodity prices and the conditions that exist in Canada at the present time.

Because the amendments which are proposed are of great interest to the farmers of southern Alberta I beg the privilege of taking up a few minutes of the time of the house. Before proceeding to give the house some suggestions based on actual examples that have recently come to my knowledge, I think I should make a short statement in all fairness to the Alberta provincial board-that is, the board that looks after farm loans in that province. As we were told this afternoon, some $15,000,000 has been provided for loans to farmers throughout the dominion, and in Alberta a very small proportion of the money has been lent to the farmers, one of the chief reasons being the provincial legislation which was enacted about the year 1926 and which we call the Debt Adjustment Act of Alberta. Should a farmer get into financial difficulties he seeks the shelter of this act and creditors find it almost impossible to obtain any of the money which they may have advanced to the farmer. Consequently the operations of the provincial farm loan board have been greatly restricted.
I will venture to present to the minister for his consideration four examples that have come to my notice from farmers living in my riding. The first relates to loans on irrigated lands. Most of these lands are held of course under agreements of sale, but we have a goodly number of farmers living on Canadian Pacific Railway lands, holding title to their farm lands, some to the extent of 320 acres. They own this land outright and the only tax which they have to pay outside of school taxes is the annual irrigation tax amounting to $1 an acre. Li%'ing within four miles of Lethbridge there is a farmer who owns 160 acres of irrigable land to which he holds free

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Stewart (Lethbridge)
title. On this land he has a magnificent brick house and a bam which would do credit to any farm in Ontario; and yet, although he has to pay only $160 a year water rental, he is not in a position to have his application for a loan considered by the Alberta board. There are quite a number of farmers in southern Alberta similarly situated and it seems to me that the government should take this example into consideration and alleviate that condition. That man surely is entitled to get his loan at five per cent just the same as any other farmer living in southern Alberta.
The second example is one with which I am very familiar. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) this afternoon mentioned a similar example in his own constituency. In the southern part of the riding I represent there is a farmer who owns 2,000 acres of land. He has a home that cost him at least $6,000, in which there is every electrical convenience to be found in Ottawa. His barns are lighted by electricity, he has at least 30 horses,
515.000	worth of machinery, and he owns the
2.000	acres outright, without one cent of mortgage or debt against the property. Moreover, he has made the money with which to purchase this land in the very district in which he now lives, and yet he cannot get one cent by way of loan from the Canadian farm loan board. Why? Because he lives in what is known as the drought area. I have known him for twenty-seven years and he has never had a crop failure and has enjoyed a good standard of living. Notwithstanding what has been said by some hon. members in this house, some of the farmers in southern Alberta, in fact a goodly number of them, enjoy a good standard of living even in these hard times. In order to meet the present unfavourable situation the farmer goes to the bank, and with all these assets, and not owing a dollar, he borrows in the neighbourhood of $2,000 and is charged seven per cent. They discount the note, and when he renews it three months afterwards it is again discounted. That situation should be taken care of. No man could have that estate in southern Alberta, accumulated in twenty-seven years, even though in a semi-dry district, without having had at least good average crops. And he comes from one of the best Scottish settlements in the dominion-I leave hon. members to draw their own conclusion as to where that may be. The one thing he does not want to do is to put a mortgage on his home, because he has never had one yet. But owing to circumstances over which he has no control he desires a loan, and yet with assets amounting to $40,000 or $50,000 he cannot get a dollar.
A little distance away from that gentleman there is another farmer residing in southern Alberta who has complained to me about the operation of the act. This gentleman bought two half sections for which he paid $30 an acre, or $9,600 each. One he bought in 1917 and one in 1918. On the one which he bought in 1917 he has paid $8,580 odd and he still owes over $9,000; on the other half section he has paid $9,800 and still owes over $8,000. In seventeen years in the one case he has made an average payment in interest or principal of over $500 per annum. It ought to be a pretty good country in which to live when a man can maintain his home and family and still be able to pay off that amount of interest or principal each year. In the other case he has paid off an average of $600 per annum. During all this time he has kept up the payment of taxes on those two half sections; each year he has given at least from one-third to one-half of the crop to the parties from whom he purchased the land and he has bought $12,000 worth of machinery. I would like to inform the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that there arp some good sections in southern Alberta, chiefly in the Lethbridge riding. This farmer goes before the official receiver and possibly may eventually get to the board of review in regard to compromising his debts. He is a good Canadian citizen. In the seventeen and eighteen years he has paid nearly $18,000 in interest and principal on those two half sections and he still owes that much more. He can never under any such conditions as prevail at the present time pay off that loan; he must get some help, and when he comes to the board of review or the official receiver he finds that he cannot get any loan from that organization.
As many hon. members have already stated, these two bills are companion measures. There must in my opinion be provision made by amendments either to this act or to the act concerning compromises with creditors, whereby a man similarly situated to this farmer will be able to get assistance to enable him to pay off his debts if he receives a reasonable adjustment. Where should he apply for this assistance if he does not go to the farm loan board?
The fourth case is similar to some that were mentioned this afternoon. There is in another part of my riding a widow who had almost enough boys to make up a full baseball team
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Reid

For thirty years they lived in southern Alberta. As the boys grew up they wished to get farms of their own and wanted to buy land in the immediate neighbourhood. The older boys succeeded in buying their farms and securing each a half section, but the two younger ones now find themselves in the position where although they have the machinery, the power and all the implements required to carry on scientific farming, they lack the capital to enable them to make a purchase of or a payment on some land which they now have under option and on which they would make their homes. It seems to me that bona fide Canadians who have been reared in our country, especially those who have been reared in Alberta and who know the conditions there, should be given an opportunity to purchase farms and get the money at a reasonable figure in order that they may be able to become the good substantial citizens they hope to be. These four cases are fair examples of those which have come under my observation and which I hope will all be covered by the legislation which is now before the house.

I desire to make a few remarks on the resolution now before the house in connection with amendments to the Farm Loan Act. At the outset let me say that I agree heartily with the observations of other members who have spoken about the high interest rates; I also have come across them in my travels through the lower Fraser valley, and they are working a very severe hardship, shall I say, on the farmers of that district. I listened attentively this afternoon while some angles of the subject were under discussion. Still there were some aspects which were not touched upon at all, and these I would like briefly to mention.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), if I interpret him aright, in speaking about the cost of borrowing said that it might take one per cent to be a safe coverage, but that it was estimated that two per cent plus the cost of borrowing would be necessary to carry out safely the operations of the act. I believe I interpret him correctly in that regard, but I wonder whether he has taken into account the question of equity. While it is true that it may take one per cent to be a safe coverage so far as the financial end of the matter is concerned, I just wonder whether the minister has thought about the equity that the farm loan board has in these farms. In connection with that I might point out that the situation in the lower Fraser valley to-day is that the equity of the farmers is

completely gone, but the equity of the government through the farm loan board still remains. Let me cite one case; many could be cited, but the one I am going to give illustrates the point I am endeavouring to make. This farmer has 812,000 cash equity in his farm, which was valued at one time at something like $18,000. To-day the equity of the board in the land which the man has is $4,110. If the farm were sold on the market at this time at a price similar to that at which neighbouring farms are selling, it would not bring more than perhaps $5,000; but it would bring $5,000, because, as I pointed out, some $18,000 have been expended and the present proprietor or owner has put into that farm some $12,000 in cash. I wonder whether the minister has considered the situation that the farm loan board of the government is adequately safeguarded in regard to land while the equity of those under the act is at the present moment at least entirely gone. That some notice has been taken by the board of falling revenues is evident, I might point out, from the fact that when farm values started to go down the farm loan board demanded more security, and if in their estimation the security was not considered sufficient they put a chattel mortgage on the stock. I would like to say in regard to this action that while it is very true that a mortgage on the land is bad enough to carry, it is certainly crucifying the farmer when he is not allowed to sell stock owing to the fact that the government through the farm loan board have a mortgage on it. That phase of the matter should be looked into and chattel mortgages removed so that the farmer, if he sees fit, will be able to sell any stock off his farm. Land values have gone down, as I pointed out, from a value of $250 an acre in 1928 to around $75 an acre. As I have already pointed out, the total security of the board is still in existence.
Something was said this afternoon regarding the five per cent share capital which the farmer is charged out of his loan. I noticed when the minister was reading the resolution that he spoke of that being done away with in the future and the share capital put up by the various provinces being returned to them. This is not the proper time to ask questions, perhaps, but I should like to know what is going to be done about the share capital that the farmers have in the various loans. I should like to read the notice sent out regarding share capital, because it is striking in view of a comparison with share capital in any business organization. This farmer had a loan of over $4,000. The notice says;

Farm, Loan Act-Mr. Reid
You are also shown as the holder of 215 paid-up shares of the capital stock of a par value of $1 pei share.
Most people if they own shares in a company look for some return by way of profit, but the very reverse is the case with farmers who have obtained a loan under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. Not only was five per cent deducted from the loan and shares issued to them, but in turn they were called upon to pay interest on the shares. In discussing the matter with farmers in my district I find that they feel very badly about having to pay interest on shares which they never owned. Before I left to come to Ottawa some twenty-five farmers gathered in the municipal hall at Cloverdale, and asked me to attend the meeting. I found that each and every one of them felt that it is the interest that is crushing them out of existence. I am not going into the question of low prices for farm produce at this time and the inability of farmers to pay; I think that is only too well known. But when we find farmers who in past years have paid their interest and their principal and have kept up their taxes, municipal and dyking and otherwise and who find that they now owe S500 and over for interest on a loan of S4,000, it is little wonder that they feel very much discouraged. As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Ooote) pointed out, some farmers who have been paying in the past and have struggled to keep up their payments feel that if others are not going to pay neither should they. It is only with great difficulty that they have met payments, denying themselves many things in order to do so, while others are not paying at all, and because they cannot.
In connection with the five per cent share capital I was wondering if this would be coming back to 'the farmer. I make this suggestion to the minister: that note be taken of the share capital which was in the first instance deducted from the loans now outstanding and that this amount be deducted from the total interest owed. That would be a great help to the farmers at the present time. Then there is the question of solicitors' fees that I think should be looked into. I know that in registering mortgages in the land registry office there are some costs, but in my opinion there is no reason why a farmer should have to pay S15 to a lawyer for making out the papers in connection with a mortgage to the farm loan board.
Speaking now in regard to the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Debt Adjustment Act, I might point out that so far as British
Columbia is concerned these two acts are niot in accord. No doubt most hon. members will remember that when the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was before the house the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) changed the definition of the word "farmer." In the Canadian Farm Loan Act the definition of "farmer" is somewhat different from that found in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. When it was under discussion last year those of us who come from British Columbia pointed out that to enable farmers on small holdings, five and ten acre men, to come under the act the word "farmer" would have to be defined differently, so it was changed to read:
"Farmer" means a person whose principal occupation consists in farming or the tillage of the soil.
It was thought that would cover the five and ten acre men in British Columbia. But in the Canadian Farm Loan Act it is not so clearly defined. It reads:
"Farming" includes stock raising, dairying and the tillage of the soil.
So we find that when those in the greenhouse business or the poultry business in British Columbia apply for a loan they are told that those in the greenhouse business or perhaps growing vegetables on five-acre holdings do not come within the act as at present constituted. I invite the minister's attention to that in order that the Canadian Farm Loan Act may be changed to conform to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in that respeot.
Regarding valuation, the creditors act passed last year has nob worked out as many of us thought it would. I am going to cite two cases from the lower Fraser valley to show that under present arrangements it is almost impossible for a farmer to obtain an adjustment under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. To quote only one or two cases, one man had a mortgage of $9,000, which he had obtained in fairly good times. Finding himself in great difficulty last year he looked around for relief. He appealed to the mortgage company and the company said: "If you can procure $4,500 we will accept that in lieu of the $9,000"; that is, they agreed to cut the mortgage in two. So he went to the official in charge of the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, who suggested that he apply to the farm loan board for a loan. But according to the valuation provisions in the Canadian Farm Loan Act the greatest amount that the board would loan

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Mills
that man was S4,000, because the valuation in British Columbia must not exceed $100 per acre, and the loan must not be over fifty per cent of the valuation, plus twenty per cent on the buildings. Therefore that man was denied the opportunity to save the 84,500.
The other case was that of a man who had a mortgage of $6,000, and the mortgage company agreed to take $3,000. But he found himself in difficulty in an endeavour to procure $3,000 from the farm loan board, although if he could have raised that money he would have saved $3,000. and had his loan cut in two. I suggest that that condition be taken into consideration and the two acts brought into conformity. I have no particular fault to find with the board or 'the officers of the board; they are servants of the crown carrying out their duties and doing their work in a businesslike way, and of course they must conform to the provisions of the act. An.y changes should be made by parliament, and now is the time to make them.
Now I should like to make a suggestion to the minister with regard to appraisals. Ten dollars may seem a small amount to have to put up, but to a man who is going around looking for a loan it is a considerable amount. It is evident 'that if he is looking for a loan he has very little money, and ten dollars represents quite a sum. So I am going to make this suggestion to the minister: why not have the appraisals made by officials of the soldier settlement board, who are doing all the appraising in the Fraser valley? That is no new departure. We have the Canadian pensioners and those under the British ministry being examined by the same doctors. The old country soldiers in Canada go before the same Canadian doctors that examine Canadian soldiers, and the same principle could be worked out in regard to appraisals. If these could be done by the soldier settlement board appraisers it would save at least $10 to each applicant.
I am going to reserve what further remarks I have to make until the bill is before us, but I should like to repeat that the most serious heavy interest charges. There is no doubt problem confronting the farmer to-day is the that something will have to be done; when a man owes $600 in interest on a $4,000 loan certainly he needs some help. That becomes aiore difficult to pay as time goes on, because it is like a snowball rolling down hill; it gets larger all the time. If something is not done many of these men will simply leave the land and lose all they ever possessed.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this opportunity pass without adding a few words to what has been said already in regard to this resolution. I believe if the governments of Canada-and when I say "governments" I mean provincial and dominion governments-are to bring prosperity back to this country they must start at the foundation, and that foundation is the farmer, the tiller of the soil. Assistance must be given the farmer.
Reference has been made by some hon. gentlemen opposite who represent constituencies in the province of Ontario to the plight of the farmers in this province, and I should like to say a word with regard to the development board that has been in operation in Ontario; for I do not believe any hon. member within sound of my voice knows more than I do of the situation that has existed in this province since the present government came into office. In reference to that board, what were the conditions the present government found when they assumed office? They found stacks of applications that had been passed by the Henry government; everything had been done with the exception of writing out the cheques and passing over the money. They found that loans had been made to 18,000 farmers in Ontario, totalling some $51,000,000, though if they had to be liquidated at the present time they would not realize $15,000,000. I do not say that is any particular fault of the Heniry government; you cannot blame a valuator for placing a value in 1028 or 1929 which was almost double the value that would be placed to-day. However, those were the conditions the new government found. It was said that no loans have been made by the new Ontario government. I should like to repeat what my hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Campbell) said, that seventy-two loans were made during November and December, totalling in the neighbourhood of $140,000. Those loans were made to applicants whose applications had been received and approved before the previous government went out of office.
Now I am going to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) that if this is to be a purely federal undertaking a great deal of care should be taken in selecting the personnel of the board that will administer it, so that politics may not creep into the administration. If I were a member of a government which appointed a commission to administer an act of this kind, and if I interfered to the extent of recommending a

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Bury
loan that had been refused by the board and that was not justified, I would not consider myself worthy of the seat I occupied. I might say here that politics did play a prominent part in connection with the administration of this act in the province of Ontario.
I cannot help thinking of the conditions that exist in my immediate neighbourhood. My constituency is purely rural, with the exception of a town and a city. Unless we have prosperity among our farmers there will not be prosperity in our town and city. We have to get those farmers back on their feet, or they will be in the bread line. I know of several good farmers in my own neighbourhood who require a little assistance, which they cannot obtain from private individuals or loan companies. A farmer hardly gets a *cordial look to-day if he appeals to a bank for a loan. I am thinking of a farmer in my locality who bought a farm some years ago at a high price, and who has raised a family of eight children. A few years ago he went to the man from whom he had bought the farm, and who held the mortgage, and asked if he could not lower the interest rate a little. The mortgage holder replied, "No, I cannot do it. I can buy government bonds and clip off coupons and get nearly six percent. I cannot take less than six per cent." I think we must get a lower interest rate because with his present income the farmer cannot meet his overhead.
I should like to tell the house of another couple whom I visited last week end when I was home. They telephoned and wanted to talk to me in reference to a farm loan. This young man had had a position in the shops at Galt, I believe. He lost his position and came home, and has been attempting to redeem the farm held by his father, which had a mortgage amounting to practically what the farm is worth to-day, because farms are not. being sold at any price.
On this farm there are good buildings, a new barn and two silos. When he came to the place he had only a small amount of stock, while to-day he has a first class accredited herd of Jerseys. However, he is up against an interest rate of seven per cent. His wife said to me, "If we could obtain a loan bearing an interest rate of 4 per cent I would feel we were right in heaven." I should like to urge that the Minister of Finance make it possible to put loans through at four per cent or less. To-day, in view of the low prices received for farm commodities, these high rates of interest cannot be met.
On my farm we are to-day producing over 600 pounds of milk daily. To deliver that milk to the condenser we are charged nine cents per hundred. This milk, rated at 3-5 per cent butterfat, is selling at $1 per hundred. With bran costing S27 or S28 per ton and other feeds at proportionately high prices, one cannot sell milk at that low price and make a profit. As the old saying goes, the farmer is the only man who can continue to do business at a loss.
May I observe in closing that I shall be pleased to support any measure which will be of assistance to the farmers or which will be the means of getting them money at a lower rate of interest, no matter from what party it comes-whether it be the government, the Liberal party or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We have to get money for our farmers; we must lend them money because they cannot borrow it elsewhere, and before they can get it we must see that it is available at a low rate of interest.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) must be gratified at the amount of interest his resolution has aroused, the amount of debate it has occasioned and the amount of approval it has elicited from both sides of the house. I hesitate delaying passage of the resolution, but I believe I must do so in order to bring to the notice of the house and the minister one concrete case which to my mind indicates a certain weakness in the present law, a weakness which the minister may not have considered and one which I hope he will be prepared to remedy.
There is a saying in the legal profession that hard cases make bad law, and we recognize the truth of that statement. The case I have to submit to the house is more than a hard case; it is one which in my opinion must be representative of a considerable number of cases. It is an instance not merely of hardship but in a certain sense of injustice which in my opinion ought to be remedied. I refer to a farmer who for thirty years farmed in eastern Canada and for seventeen years farmed first in Saskatchewan and afterwards in Alberta. He owns a section farm three miles from the town of Erskine and one mile from the wheat pool elevator. Some years ago, by reason of an accident to his spine, he became paralyzed, and had to leave his farm and reside in the city of Edmonton, where he still lives. Notwithstanding his paralysis and his age he has been operating his farm from his bed. A man has been working the farm under his absolute control and direction, and
42S
COMMOJNs
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Gershaw
he has been paying for the seed and meeting the other costs in connection with putting in the crops. There is an arrangement between the two men whereby the man working the farm gets fifty per cent of the crop for his work. A few years ago the farm was valued at about $25,000. There are 475 acres under cultivation, good buildings and good fencing. For these reasons that valuation would not appear to be at all exorbitant. Since 1930 the owner in Edmonton has fallen into arrears with his taxes. To put in his 1931 crop he had to borrow from the bank. The amount of his indebtedness to the bank plus the amount of his taxes is $3,500; yet he cannot obtain a loan from the farm loan board because he happens to live in Edmonton, paralyzed on a bed, and is not living on the farm.
Hon. members will recall that some years ago a bonus of five cents per bushel was given on the wheat produced.
