In the spring of the year in which the bonus was paid he borrowed from the bank for the purpose of putting in his crop. He had ploughed 100 acres of summer fallow, had broken 34 acres of new land, and his borrowing from the bank was at an interest rate of eight per cent. In that year of 1931 he raised a crop of 6,000 bushels. Applying for the five cents bonus he was told that because he was not living on the land he could not have it; the man who did the actual work of raising the crop got the whole of the five centa bonus on the 6,000 bushels, while the owner in Edmonton did not get a cent. I am inclined to believe, from memory, that in point of fact there is an agreement of sale executed in favour of the man who put in the crop, and if that is the case difficulties would be possible. The point I wish to urge upon the minister, however, is that there should be a greater margin of discretion or wider powers given to meet cases such as this. In this instance the man is actually operating the farm, although the house in which he lives is at a distant point. His lifetime's savings are in that farm, and to-day I am not sure but what it has been sold for taxes. He entered into the ordinary consolidation of tax arrears agreement and made two payments since. 1930. but has not been able to make further payments since. The result is that bis tax agreement is in default and his protection under the consolidation agreement has gone. This man is a helpless cripple in possession of a valuable farm. It is possible, if not an actuality, that his farm may be sold for $1,000 or $1,500 arrears in taxes. I urge upon the minister that the definition of the term 
"farmer" should be widened so as to make provision for such cases. If he has not sold the farm I would urge and press and contend that the mere fact that he is living in Edmonton does not make him a non-occupant of the farm, and that even then he is within the definition of a farmer under the Farm Loan Act. But even if he has sold the farm, surely it should not be impossible to make some provision in the act that men who have a really valuable equity in a farm and who have for so many years been working at farming and building up the prosperity of the east or the west, should in some measure be protected, and that some relief and some concessions should be made to them in some way to enable them to get the money that is necessary to enable this man I speak of and others like him to avert a complete loss of the earnings and toil of his lifetime I do not know how the amendment can be made, but I do suggest that it might be made in some way. In the 1934 amendment to this act provision was made under section 10 of part II that a loan might be made to a mortgagee who is defined as "any loan, trust or insurance company," and that term is extended to include " such other corporations or persons or classes of corporations or persons" as might be designated by the governor general in council, on the security of an assignment or hypothecation of a first mortgage; and that term is defined as including an agreement of sale covering lands the title to which is in the mortgagee, using the term mortgagee in the wide sense. Now if such can be done in that case, why cannot it be done in the ordinary case of an application for a loan? I made application for this man a couple of years ago, I remember, and it was turned down on the ground that he was not actually an occupant of these lands.

Mr. Speaker, a good deal of what I intended to say has already been said, and I shall certainly not repeat it. I notice in looking over the statement that the farm loan board has not sustained many heavy losses, and the number of cases in which interest or principal payments are in arrears is not very great.
A few days ago I put a question on the order paper and by the answer I notice that fewer and fewer loans are being made year after year. For instance, in the province of Alberta in 1931 the number of loans was 298; in 1932, 239; and in 1933 the number was 80, and in 1934 the number had dropped to 47. I also asked what areas in the province were excluded from the operation of this act, and the answer I received was this:

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Golding
None. The policy of the board is to deal with applications on the basis of the productive value of the security offered and the qualifications of the applicant.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, when people in the southern part of the province apply for a loan they are invariably told that no loans are being considered in that district. We cannot blame tire board for being veiy careful with their loans because we know that year after year disaster has overtaken the crops in part of that district, but even in that blanket area where no loans are considered there are farms that annually have produced fairly good crops. There are farmers living in ithe hills who have been getting on reasonably well and who have every right to have their application for a loan, when they require it, considered.
Then again, as has been said, this act works in with the farmers' debt adjustment act. I would point out to the minister the futility of having commissioner's appointed and acting under the farmers' debt adjustment act in a district where there is no possibility of getting a loan from the farm loan board. When the act is being amended I do hope the minister will see his way clear to extend its scope to save some of the homes which are being lost at the present time. In the city whence I come a large number of retired farmers have made payments on their homes in the city and have counted on making future payments from the revenue from their farms. But they have been disappointed in getting that revenue and have been unable to meet their obligations, and consequently stand to lose their homes. Some are now tenants on their own property, and others, of course, will be forced to vacate their property in the near future. I believe that this is a field of activity which might well be added to an act such as this, and if that could be accomplished it would dispel the despair which some of these people feel, and in its place bring some courage and confidence and contribute greatly to the happiness and contentment of the Canadian people.
Mr. WILLIAM H. GOLDING (South Huron): Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity of expressing my views on this question and of endorsing the views expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott). I think that any member who represents a rural constituency and spends any time at all among his constituents must understand the distress and worry that our agriculturists are experiencing at the present time and have been for the last three or four years. I am very glad indeed
that the house has devoted the time it has this afternoon and evening to what since I have been a member of this house I have often considered as the forgotten man. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are going on adding to our machinery of government. An unemployment insurance scheme is now proposed, also an economic council; we have our marketing board, and whether we believe it or not, all these cost money to administer. After all, these costs find their way back to the consumer and to the basic producer, and ultimately in my opinion to our greatest industry, that of agriculture.
I have often wondered since I have been a member of this house, and it has given me a great deal of concern, just how long we can continue to add to our machinery of government and place these burdens upon the backs of our farmers who already are overburdened and have been for years.
Take the unemployment insurance scheme, for instance. No doubt it is a good thing in itself, and yet I can see that it is going to place another burden upon the farmers' backs. I think that every manufacturer who has to do with the agriculturists will recognize that all the costs that go into the upkeep of that scheme will have to be passed on to the agriculturists. In my own constituency during last fall and this winter I have been approached on a good many occasions in regard to the Farm Loan Act and the debt adjustment plan. Of course, in Ontario that is not yet in effect but I think it will be; enabling legislation will be passed as soon as the legislature meets. But I do want to add my plea to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to do everything in his power to see that this interest is reduced even to four per cent. Practically every member in this house would, I think, be quite willing to see the government take care of any interest charges over that amount. I have a feeling that a movement of that kind would be supported. We have had loans to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I suppose the government can justify those loans; we have bad guarantees to that railway of $60,000,000. When we do that kind of thing I cannot see for the life of me why we cannot do something just as good and big for our agriculturists.
I do not wish to traverse the ground that has been so well covered by various speakers who have preceded me, but as the representative of a rural constituency I want to plead with the Minister of Finance and with the government to do all that lies in their power to have these loans available at four per cent,
43U
Farm Loan Act-Air. Blair

and I am sure our farmers all through the country would be greatly pleased if that could be brought about.
My only regret is that action of this kind was not taken two or three years ago. I can assure the house that so far as this action at the present time is concerned, it is too late for a great many of the farmers in my constituency, men who have come to me in the last two years to tell me about their difficulties and their troubles. But while that is true, I say let us take action now and do something that will benefit the people who are engaged in what in my opinion is the greatest industry in the dominion.

While I approve very much of the proposal that is before us, I wish to bring to the attention of the house certain abuses that prevail in the district from which I come. We find that when a mortgage is higher than the value of the farm some banker, some loan company or some real estate man having charged a high rate of interest so that the mortgage value is greatly in excess of the farm value, then they get the farmer and his friends together and they say to him, "We will get you a loan on this from the government." They get a loan on the farm for much more than it is worth and then burden the neighbouring farmer by paying more for the farm than its value, with no intention of paying the mortgage but leaving the farm the next year. This has been done in many instances to the detriment of neighbouring farmers.
In the county I represent the farmers find it almost impossible to get a mortgage on their farms. It was bad enough when the provincial government offered five per cent for their loans, but when they offered six per cent that ruined farm loans almost entirely, because the farmer found it impossible to get a loan. We find therefore in North Wellington that there are bams without shingles, houses needing repairs, fences down and cattle in the grain here and there. The farmers are in a desperate situation for lack of money. They require implements but they are unable to buy them. Implements that should have been discarded years ago they are bound to continue using. Another great hardship is their handicap in producing revenue. Their horses and cattle have been reduced in numbers, and sometimes they have had to sell the best of them to raise money to meet interest.
I do not think that four per cent is too low; the lower we can get it the better. The wages of money should have some relationship to the wages of men, and the man who has a

farm does not get four per cent on his investment. Practically speaking, the farmers today are working without wages but only for their keep. We want the interest rate as low as possible.

I
cannot agree with the last speaker (Mr.. Blair). Possibly he has a little money out drawing a high rate of interest and feels that he would not like to have anything less. But in my constituency there are a good many people who will join with some members on the other side in advocating a rate of interest as low as they can obtain. I feel proud of the fact that I belong to a party that has the courage to undertake the task of reinstating the farmer. It is one of the greatest measures we have had before us, and I do not hesitate to say that it is approved by all the farmers in my constituency.
It was suggested by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Campbell) that the late provincial government was trying to collect a high rate of interest. If I understood him correctly, he intimated that they were charging six per cent or thereabouts. As long as I can remember, for quite a number of years, the Ontario board was lending money at five and a half per cent, and in fact that was the only source from 'which you could get money. If my hon. friend will look up the records he will find that the late government notified all their loan holders in June last that the rate of interest would be reduced to four and a half per cent. If the present government lends at four per cent that will be better still and will be quite agreeable to my constituency, as no doubt it will be to the constituency which the hon. gentleman represents. At the same time the late government should get the credit that it deserves, because a great deal was done in my locality.
The hon. gentleman went so far as to say that the late government had practically thrown away the money, carelessly allowing interest to accrue here and there. I would point out to him that the very same thing would happen if he had the reins of power. These loan boards were compelled to take chattel mortgages on the stock which the men had, but as there was no way in which they could possibly sell the stock to raise taxes there was only one thing for the tax collector to do, and that was to return the tax bill to the county against the property.
The hon. member suggested that the Ontario government had lent several thousand dollars since they came into office. This

Farm. Loan Act-Mr. Beynon
may be true, but it depends upon what side you are on. However, let it be where it is, it makes no difference so long as the loan does some good, because the man who applies for a loan needs it or he would not try to get one. Far be it from me to make capital out of this matter, because this is something that concerns every man in the rural districts. I do not quite agree with the hon. member opposite when he says that this legislation is too late. Even if it is coming along in the last days of this parliament, I admire a government that has the courage to step in and do something. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that these things should have been done two or three or four years ago, but the former government was in power for a long time and yet it did nothing. The present government is giving action and action at once so that we will get relief, and there has been no time that we needed it any worse than we do to-day.
As regards the suggestion that those loans were given very carelessly and that some received more than they should, surely my hon. friends opposite do not think that the men who made the valuations were not fair valuators. While they are pretty well cleared out, there are some of them in office still. Those men used good judgment. There is a great deal of difference between the days when you could sell a cow and receive enough money possibly to meet the interest, and today when you would have to sell a dozen cows to meet it, and the same thing would apply in all these cases. If hon. members would look into some of the records they would see that in those days when it was easier to pay $1,000 or $2,000 or $3,000 from the price of produce sold than it is now to pay $150, the amount at which those lands were valued was not too high. If the present provincial government spends the money as wisely as did the late one, they will not do bad business.
I do not want to take up much of the time of the house because I think we are all of about the same mind on the matter. I am sure we will all be agreeable if the interest rate is kept down, and any government that has courage enough to go ahead and introduce a measure, as I said, to reinstate the farmer at the present time, is certainly going to study the whole question and give him the money at the lowest possible rate of interest.

Just before the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) rose to speak I had intended addressing the house for a very few moments
on one branch of this subject which has not yet been touched, or at least, had not until then. I do not intend to go over those phases of the Farm Loan Act which have been dealt with. Some of the remarks I heartily concur in; others I do not, but I will leave that for the time being. We have however in all districts in this country cases similar to that stated by the hon. member for East Edmonton, some of them differing somewhat; and I want to deal with one along that line but somewhat different.
There is living in the city of Moose Jaw a gentleman who came to this country from the great republic to the south. He has been farming in that district now to my knowledge for over twenty years. He brought with him to this country over $30,000 in cash, and he invested that money in farm lands in the Moose Jaw district. He has broken those lands and improved them, and all his farms are equipped with the very best of farm buildings. They are also all supplied with the very best of farm machinery and ample power to work them. This man, who had acquired over $30,000 in farming in the United States and who has since then been conducting several large farms in this country, is no longer a young man; consequently he has moved into the city and is living there while his sons and sons-in-law are operating those farms. During this time of drought in that part of the country it has cost a great deal to keep the farms going and his reserves have been pretty well exhausted. He has been buying seed, helping the boys to put in their crops and trying to provide a living for himself. When he was actually farming there was not a year that he could not have had a loan of $5,000 or $10,000 from the bank without any question whatever. This year he went to the bank to borrow a few hundred dollars to pay his taxes and they would not give him a dollar. This man is the owner in his own right of several sections of land, all clear and with the very best of farm buildings. The fact that he is not residing on the land, not actually farming, takes him outside the terms of this act, although he is responsible for the operation of the farms. He is not alone in this; there are many men in that city who are in the same situation, and I have talked to a number of them. The case is very similar to the one stated by the hon. member for East Edmonton. What these men want is not a loan for twenty or thirty years, but a short term loan at a reasonable rate of interest, something to carry them over until they can get a crop and look after themselves. This man unfortunately was hailed out this year.
432	COMMONS
Farm Loan Act-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
Had it not been for that unfortunate fact, notwithstanding the drought in that district, he would have had sufficient to pay his taxes and cany on his farming operations. It is that class of people who have come and lived here, built up this country, spent a great deal of money, who are to-day denied any source from which they can get money to keep them alive. This man has not a thing on which to keep up his house in the city except what he gets off the farm. I assume they had perhaps a little to sell off the farm, but he needs some money now to put in seed and carry him for the time being.
If the minister could arrange somewhere in this legislation to provide for short term credits for men of this class

not fly-by-night men, but men who have been here for years, men who have built up the country and are substantial citizens-I think that is what should be done. I just want to bring this matter to the attention of the minister because it is a point that should be dealt with, and it has not been covered in recent speeches.

I listened with a great deal of interest this afternoon to the minister when he introduced this resolution proposing amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I think we can all apprehend a general acceptance of the resolution as introduced. Apparently there was quite general unanimity with respect to the object of the proposed amendments to the act. It goes without saying that they will virtually revolutionize the mortgage loan business of the country, and the dominion government in the very near future will be the sole institution lending money on farm lands. That may be all right. It is a huge step and I can quite appreciate that it may be even more acceptable to the farmers themselves than it will be to members of parliament after this legislation becomes operative.
I can see considerable objection to the old act as to the manner in which it operated, in that it was not applicable in or used by all the provinces. I think that may have been unfair. As regards the proposal to consolidate the administration of the act in Ottawa through provincial offices, I have no complaint or observation to make. Perhaps that will work for more uniform administration. In the meantime I should just like to say that so far as the organization in Manitoba is concerned I have not heard of any particular complaint against the officers operating there.
Except in Souris.

There was no
complaint there. With regard to amending the part of the act which required the borrower to subscribe for stock in the company to the extent of five per cent, I am glad to see that eliminated. It used to be in the mind of many people interested in farm loans and rural credits that we should try by this means to secure the interest of the men borrowing the money, with the idea that in so doing he would feel that he was part of the institution, and thereby it would operate more efficiently. But experience shows that that requirement kept a great many people from taking advantage of loans under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I recall looking into two or three proposals for loans by farmers, and it worked out that the farmer had to pay roughly S8.50 for each S100 borrowed. That looked large to him, so he naturally looked elsewhere for his money. The minister stated this afternoon, if I heard him correctly, that the money subscribed by the . provincial governments up to date would be returned to them. The question came to my mind, as it did to that of another hon. member who spoke: what about the five per cent already advanced by farmers who have taken advantage of these loans? I should like to see that money returned to the fanners in the form of credits on their interest or arrears.
There are two other features to which I should like to refer. In this respect I may get into deep water, but it seems to me that in view of the debt adjustment legislation and prior claims and things of that kind that have developed in the last ten or fifteen years in respect to farm mortgages, our whole farm loan policy will have to be considerably changed. The two features that I should like to submit for the minister's consideration are with respect to the personal covenant and the right to repay a loan at any time without bonus. As far as the personal covenant is concerned my feeling is that it should not be required on a farm mortgage. You might say it should not apply to the homesteader.
I have in mind a farmer owning say a half section of land. Personally I feel that that is a nice sized little farm. He may have that clear of debt. But sometimes we ge't ambitious and wish to add more land. When it comes to purchasing that additional land and borrowing money for the purpose from any mortgage corporation I feel that the farmer should be protected to the extent that his personal covenant should not go on that new loan: in other words protect him to keep him on the homestead.

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
As to the bonus, if a loan should be paid before due I would submit that the minister might make provision to accept the principal of the loan at any time that it is available. We have seen too many cases in the past in which before a loan came due a man might have had a particularly good year and was in a position to pay off his loan, yet because he had to pay an additional amount to get the mortgage company to take that money he refrained from paying it. Human nature just made him take the position that he would not pay any bonus to the mortgage company. That money then was probably not used to the best advantage, and perhaps when the mortgage finally came due it was not there.
This measure will provide that the dominion government may loan to the farmers of Canada up to $90,000,000. That is a lot of money. Of course it is going to operate in conjunction with the debt adjustment legislation passed a year ago; that is all to the good. I suggest to the minister that an effort be made to have this legislation put into operation as soon as possible. I have in mind people preparing to put in a crop this year. If they could feel assured that they could secure money in the way of a loan at a lowT rate of interest from this organization, they would be much more encouraged to go ahead and put in the crop, and at the same time, where they are heavily involved, would have the additional advantage of making a more satisfactory adjustment with their creditors.
One serious difficulty is with respect to the valuation of land. I cannot tell you how you could go out and value farm lands in Manitoba to-day, and I assume the same thing applies to the other provinces. I listened to what the bon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) said with respect (to loans in his district. He referred to the farm loan board lending money in another district that suffered from flooding a few years ago. This district since that time has suffered for three years considerable grasshopper damage-not a total loss in every instance but many farmers having practically a total loss for the past five years. I have in mind an illustration. I am reminded of a fanner near me who had a first class quarter section of land. He did not live on it, and consequently was not able to borrow money on it from the farm loan board. He had purchased it under an agreement of sale. Last fall he owed $2,300 on that quarter section. The man to whom he owed the money said, "K you can get me $1,000 I will call it square." and he had to beg friends to let him 92582-28
have that $1,000 at six per cent interest. I recall what he told me of one man whom he approached for a loan. The man said to him, "Why should I lend you $1,000 on that quarter section when I can go down into the district where my own lands are and buy a quarter section from the municipality for $750?" Now, the quarter section that he could buy for $750 is in the area which was flooded out some years ago and to which my hon. friend from Souris referred. So the difficulty of placing a valuation on farm lands for mortgage purposes is very great. I know of many farms in my own district carrying mortgages as high as $20 an acre. Of course this man who was able to pay off his $2,300 mortgage with $1,000 was pleased to do it- Perhaps that might be called the purifying effect of capitalism and regarded as one of its advantages. In that connection may I point out that it is likely that some day the government will be obliged to accept a less amount of money for mortgages than the amount loaned.	'
I think the government is fortunate in being ahle to start this plan at this time. Farm lands are undoubtedly low in price now, and the risks should be proportionately less. In Manitoba we had the Manitoba Farm Loan Association, which unfortunately started at a bad time. Its history is not any too bright. I hope that this legislation will meet with much greater success. The fact of its being started in a period of depressed prices should make for success.
There is one other point that comes to my mind, and it is this; if I recall correctly the aict as it stands at present provides for one per cent additional interest on arrears. I do submit that this should be changed. The man who farms or wants to farm is anxious to keep up his payments if possible, and I submit to the minister that if it can be done some provision should be made for carrying arrears, if they must occur, at the original rate of interest.
The other feature that comes to my mind is that it does seem too bad, when we can secure money at four per cent or perhaps less, that we have to add one per cent for administrative costs. That seems too high a percentage for that service. It may be necessary but it does not seem fair, in comparison with the cost of the money, to 'have to pay an additional one per cent just to administer the organization and provide for the reserve to be set aside for bad debts.
I have nothing further to say with respect to this legislation except a word of commendation to the government. I honestly think



Farm Loan Act-Mr. Spencer
this is a move in the right direction; I feel that we are starting at the right place. I agree with other hon. members who have taken the position that after all is said and done we can talk about the assistance we must give to the unemployed, to the building trades and so on, but in the final analysis if you can get the farm business on a sound basis and in a position to carry itself reasonably well you will do more to relieve our generally distressed situation than by all the other legislation you might put through.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed that this act is to be amended in a worth while fashion. I remember when the act was passed by this house in 1926; we had great hopes in regard to this type of legislation. It was put forward as a great advance, as no doubt it was, and if the administration had been carried on in the spirit in which the act was drawn up, there is no doubt at all in my mind that it would have filled a great want. Unfortunately, however, after the act was passed it was held up for a year, and then it seemed to fall down entirely as far as administration was concerned. I say it fell down because we had hoped that at least twenty per cent of the enormous number of mortgages in Canada would have been taken up under this act. It was estimated that if this happened it would have the effect of forcing the loan companies to bring down their charges to the level of those made by the farm loan board. Owing to the way in which the act was administered, however, very little money was loaned. According to some figures given me in 1932 I find that only 4,119 loans were granted out of 14,423 applications made, and although the Minister of Finance had the right to purchase bonds of the farm loan board to the extent of 815,000,000 I find that up to 1932 only 87,500,000 had been loaned under the act.
I knew that the act was not working out successfully in the province from which I come, so far as loans were concerned, but I was interested in the figures given to-night by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), who said that in 1931 only 298 loans were made in the province of Alberta, and the number dropped as low as 47 in 1934. It always seemed to me that one of the weaknesses in the act so far as Alberta was concerned, and I suppose this applied to other provinces as well, was that loans were not made unless the borrower turned over as security the land on which his house was

built. I know many men of excellent standing as farmers who wanted loans on land, but not on the land on which their houses stood. Although they had ample security to offer for the loans, their applications were refused. I know of several cases in which the would be borrowers, after having been turned down by the board, made application to ordinary loan companies and received advances on their land without delay.
I join with others in this house who have stressed the absolute need of a very low rate of interest under this act. I do not know what the Minister of Finance has in mind, but I sincerely hope that the rate will not be more than four per cent, and that if possible it will be less. As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) pointed out earlier in the evening, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the Farm Loan Act are two measures that should work together, but while I have great hopes of some good being done by the administration of the first measure I am rather afraid that it will be a partial failure if we do not see that the greatest possible use is made of the farm loan act.
I should like to say just a word with regard to the cost of administration. We are informed in regard to the unemployment insurance measure the government proposes to carry the cost of administration. If that is to be done in order to help those in the cities who are receiving insurance relief woidd it be too much to ask the government to carry the cost of administration of this act in order to help out those who earn their livelihood in the country?
I do not wish to say more at this time because we do not know all the details of this bill. I freely admit that we had great hopes when this act was first introduced; we have been frightfully disappointed, but at the same time I realize that if the necessary amendments are made it may become a very useful piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, if I rise at this time it is not because I desire to find fault with what the distinguished critic of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has said. I had hoped to spare the house the trouble of listening to me, but so few members from the province of Quebec have expressed their views on this important question that I fear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) may think us indifferent to his proposed legislation if something is not said by some of us who eome from this province.

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Gagnon
During this debate we have heard many new members make their maiden speeches, and certainly they deserve ito be congratulated because they have pleaded well the cause of the farmers of their constituencies. We know, of course, that they are fresh from the byelections, and undoubtedly they have come here determined to fight the government to the last ditch. It is a pleasure to the older members, however, ito realize that the newer members find it necessary, when they rise for the first time, to congratulate the government on the proposed new reforms which it is hoped will bring salvation to Canada. '
This resolution is very important indeed, in view of the sad situation of agriculture, not only in the western part of Canada but in the province of Quebec. The dire condition ?f farmers and the great poverty under which they are operating certainly cannot be overstressed. I happen to represent a rural constituency which has suffered very much during the depression, and certainly my constituents will welcome with great pleasure the amendments the government is introducing.
I have already advocated some reforms in connection with rural credits. Speaking on the budget in 1932, I said:
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to other legislation which has been disastrous to the farmers of eastern Canada; I mean the law rnacted in 1929 creating the Canadian Farm Loan Board. This legislation may have been aeneficial to the western farmers, but it has aot been at all helpful to the farmers of eastern Canada. The rate of interest is too high, the legal fees incident to the granting of loans are also too high, and the obligation laid upon borrowers to contribute to the special fund is not only unpractical but absurd.
I realize I might have used milder language, but these were my views. To illustrate the impracticability of the legislation I shall describe to the house the case of a poor farmer living in one of the older parishes in my constituency. His farm was valued at S4,000. In 1932 he applied for a loan of only 81,400 which has not yet been granted. Notwithstanding the fact that he has been unsuccessful in his effort to secure a loan, he has been sued by a notary who is charging him the sum of $400-only $400-for the cost of investigating titles, and so on. I have complained to the federal and provincial boards, but they say there is no remedy because they cannot prove that the notary did not render the services for which he has charged so high a fee.
Nevertheless I feel this case illustrates my point, namely, that the criticism which has been levelled at the act is certainly justified 92582-28J
in many respects. I believe all hon. members agree that amendments are necessary, because I have not heard any dissenting voice this afternoon from any quarter of the chamber. Of course we know that at the last session some amendments were made, but as the hon. members for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe) and Compton (Mr. Gobeil) said this afternoon, the enabling legislation has not been passed 'by the legislative assemblies of Ontario and Quebec, although in Quebec the legislature has been in session since January 7. Everyone realizes that a general overhauling of the act has to be made. I understand there are difficulties the government will have to face in connection with any change in rates of interest, but I feel I must agree with what some hon. members have said, namely that it would be highly desirable, if at all possible, to have the rate of interest lowered to four per cent.
In 1931 the Conservative opposition in Quebec waged a very extensive campaign for the establishment of a provincial system of rural credits. At that time the leader of the opposition in that province was criticized and considered very unwise because he recommended that the rate of interest should not exceed two and a half per cent. Nevertheless in some financial reviews we have read lately that in Italy Mussolini has created a system of rural credits whereby the farmers pay only two and a half per cent. I am not at all prepared to go that far now, because I realize conditions in southern and central Europe are very much different from those obtaining in America. That is true because of our longer winters, and the fact that farming in this country cannot be carried on for more than six months. Nevertheless I certainly wish the government would lower the rate of interest to as low a point as possible.
I recognize that due to pressure of public opinion the legislature in the province of Quebec has contributed one and a half per cent to the interest charged by the Canadian farm loan board. I sincerely hope when the new legislation is in operation the provincial government will see its way clear to raise its contribution to the point where they will pay half the interest levied.
May I also stress the point that one must not lose sight of the fact that the new legislation will be a necessary complement of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which only lately has been passed. In the province of Quebec the farmers have applied to the middle class, the rentiers, to obtain loans, but in many instances the rentiers are not much richer than the farmers. Some rentiers have

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Gagnon
loaned to the farmers everything they had, and now on account of moratorium legislation passed in Quebec since 1933 those creditors cannot get their money. At this time they cannot obtain relief from the banks or from the mortgage loan companies. Therefore it is necessary that they have at their disposal the only instrument from which they can get relief, namely the Canadian Farm Loan Board.
Therefore I urge the minister to set up as speedily as possible the required organization to provide the necessary moneys so that the farmers who this winter have made arrangements with their creditors may secure a loan as soon as possible next spring. I urge the minister, further, to appoint a large number of farm inspectors so that at the earliest possible moment farms may be inspected. I realize this will entail an expenditure of money, but it will not constitute a waste because the more money spent to inspect farms and provide loans to farmers the less money will be spent in the administration of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
For these reasons I am pleased to concur in what has been said from all quarters of the house in welcoming the resolution. Indeed it must be gratifying for the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister to know that the new program of reforms has been so well received by the opposition, because nothing by way of reform could be more practical than that which tends to ameliorate the conditions under which the farmers are operating.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not take
the time of the house to discuss the question of farm loans from the standpoint of their economic soundness, because experience has proven in this country and in the United States that from that point of view they have been disastrous. If I recollect aright, before the N.R.A. legislation in the United States, that country had claims against farmers for over one and a half billion dollars which were considered then a complete loss to the country; and if we consider this legislation on that ground, it certainly would be very hard to understand. But I suppose that the government in its last hour of agony has decided for once to find within its bosom one good resolution. May I hope, Mr. Speaker, that it may not prove to be one brick paving the floor of that place to which I do not wish the government to go at the next election?
I have tried to find a reason why the government is bringing down this legislation at

this late hour. I have asked myself: Is it because they have tried that other legislation called the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which they passed last year, and which as a matter of fact has completely destroyed the credit of the farmer of eastern Canada?
It was all destroyed before that law was passed.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman finds the destruction around him so extensive that everywhere he sees nothing but destruction. But speaking for the province of Quebec, from which my hon. friend comes, he knows perfectly well that before that Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed, farmer lenders in our province relied on the credit of a farmer, because they knew that no sounder or better security was to be found in Canada than the security of our farms even since the crisis. Don't shake your head.
Absolutely no.
The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) says, "absolutely no." Well, I hope he will go into his riding and say that again.
I certainly will.
Then he has more courage than judgment.
That remains to be seen.

They say he will not
come back.

In the province of Quebec
the best security was our farms before the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed, but since the enactment of that legislation there is not a single lender who would dare to lend one cent on a farm, because the farmers, good and bad, as soon as they are sued for a mortgage, now rush to the local administrator of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and seek an adjustment reducing their mortgage perhaps fifty per cent; or they may ask that they be absolved from paying interest for from fifteen to fifty years. The hon. member for Compton knows that. Who will dare to lend money on the security of the farm under those conditions? The consequence is that the farmers have their backs to the wall. They do not know what to do. There is only one recourse and it is this legislation.
Why did the government wait so long to pass this legislation? Was it because, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said in his

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Dupuis
radio addresses, the opposition deliberately opposed any legislation that the government introduced into this house in the last two or three years? I would answer the Prime Minister by saying that if the opposition did anything wrong in that particular case it was in not opposing the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Nobody said a single word against it last session, and it has proved to be the worst piece of legislation that was passed.
Weren't you here then?

I was here, but I had the same idea that the Prime Minister mentioned over the radio. I did not want to oppose the government too much because, although I am not a prophet, I knew that the Prime Minister, having no other argument, would try to throw something on the opposition one way or the other, so I think I showed good judgment, as did all the members on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has got you going all right.

This year the government comes with this legislation, and I say it is too late. It is only a deathbed repentance.
My hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), with his fine command of English, which I envy him, said: In 1932 I said such and such a thing in favour of the farmer. Well, Mr. Speaker, if I may take the attitude of a great man as he does, may I also remind the house of what the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville said, not in 1932, but in the special session of 1930 when the government put through its unemployment relief measure:
I would ask the Prime Minister if the last two lines of clause 2 of the bill, reading "for such purposes and under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council" are broad enough to permit of an amendment to the Farm Loan Act to reduce the interest rate from 6^ to 4J per cent.
In that special session in 1930, when the Prime Minister was taking the money from the purse which we had left filled with forty-four million dollars before going out of office, and spending $20,000,000, throwing it away to fulfil one of his election promises because he did not want to perish in the attempt, I thought then, as the representative of a farming constituency, that it would have been proper for the government to redeem another promise and extend that relief to the farmer, and that is why I asked the Prime Minister then to reduce the rate of interest. But did they do anything about it? No, they were deaf-but not dumb. They could not
do it then-it was impossible. If I remember well, the representatives of all the farmers of this country took the trouble, although they were starving, to make a pilgrimage to Ottawa, and mind you, among this distinguished delegation there were members of parliament, including the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) and the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). They sent three delegates to the Prime Minister, who was very busy with the big lords of England, and they disturbed the tranquillity of the right hon, gentleman when they asked him to come to the rescue of the farmer. You know very well, and the whole country knows what the Prime Minister answered. He said he did not have time to meet the delegation. They then begged him to send the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), who is as a matter of fact a real gentleman, "Oh," said the Prime Minister, "the Minister of Agriculture is as busy as I am; we have no time for that." They were here for the purpose of asking this government, at a time when it was opportune, to help the farmer. But nothing was done. As regards the rate of interest, the argument was that it could not be lowered.
I see here in a Montreal newspaper, a newspaper which is always very delicate in what it has to say with regard to members of parliament-and the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) knows something about this, because I see a nice article written on this subject-I see in this newspaper something about the three ministers from the district of Montreal. I will not dare to repeat what is said about these three ministers, because I am proud of my province; I am proud of the population of that province, and I would be ashamed to repeat it before the representatives of the whole country, and leave this house under the impression that the whole province of Quebec is on the level on which the three ministers of the crown from the province of Quebec have been placed. The only thing I want to point out is that they praise the Prime Minister, declaring that had the ministers from the province of Quebec been more active, had they exercised more influence with the Prime Minister, they could have obtained something that would help to rescue the city of Montreal. And to prove it they say, "Mr. Houde just applied to the Prime Minister and in one moment the Prime Minister found in England $6,000,000 at a rate of 3} per cent." That is all very well, but may I ask whether the influence of the right hon. gentleman could not have been used on behalf

of the most important and the most interesting class in this country, the farmers who have been starving since this government came into power?
Nevertheless the intention is good and I want to congratulate the government on bringing down this legislation. It is better than nothing. We know that Christian charity obliges us to forgive even the greatest sinner in his last hour of agony, and I do not want to be less Christian than I am bound to be.
The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) tried to throw stones at the government of the province of Quebec. Well, that is his usual habit; he is used to doing that because he has no argument against the Liberals in the federal field. But may I remind him that the province of Quebec, as he said-and I thank him for being frank for once-has contributed to the extent of one and a half per cent in the rate of interest in connection with the farm loan board. That is something. But he goes further. The hon. gentleman suggested that the province of Quebec should contribute fifty per cent of the rate of interest under this new legislation. Is it because his Prime Minister has acceded to the request of the premier of Quebec to contribute fifty per cent in connection with the unemployment relief legislation in Montreal, and by so doing relieve the municipalities of their unbearable burden, that he makes through this House of Commons a petition to the government of Quebec?
I heard the premier of Quebec about a month ago make that kind offer to the Prime Minister of Canada to contribute fifty per cent. I do not know whether I am wrong, but the Prime Minister is here to say whether I am or not. At any rate, I have never heard that the Prime Minister of Canada has accepted that offer of Premier Taschereau.

I am prepared to wait for an explanation from the Prime Minister. I should like to hear what the offer was. The Prime Minister has sometimes said that I am not clever, and I am the first to admit it. But I believe that I understand something about political economy-
Honesty.

I will not say honesty, because the Prime Minister is an honest man. But I understand something of political economy and I know something about the meaning of words. I was there the night the premier of Quebec spoke, and the speech was

broadcast. He said, "I am ready to contribute to the amount of fifty per cent if the Prime Minister of Canada is ready to contribute the same amount to relieve the municipalities of the province of Quebec of the burden which is sending them into bankruptcy." The hon. member for Dorchester no doubt knows in his heart, therefore, that the premier of Quebec is a very good administrator and made a very opportune offer, because he knows very well that the municipalities in this country are all going to be ruined if they continue to contribute one-third.

Mr. DUPU'IS: You deal with the hon. member for Beauce; he will settle you, because he knows you better than I do.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. I am in favour of this new legislation so far as I know what it is at the present time, reserving my right to discuss it on its merits when it comes 'before the house again, and I hope that the rate of interest will be as low as possible. The cost of administration is one and a half per cent for the farm loan board, and I am always asking myself why the cost of administration of the farm loan board is not paid by the government itself, because in many other commissions it is paid by the government. For instance, as regards the natural products marketing board, the railway board, the unemployment insurance board and perhaps many others, their administration is paid by the government, and I do not see why the farmers of this country are not of as much importance as those concerned with all this other class of business. I just put this question to the government. If this one and a half per cent is taken away from the rate of interest already intended to be charged, a great benefit will ensue to the farmers, and this may help to cover the bad features of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
Mr. CAMERON R. MoINTOSH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, I desire to make just a few (Observations in connection with the resolution before the house. Perhaps the background of this resolution is somewhat similar to the background of the Agricultural Adjustment Act and the National Industrial Recovery Act characterizing the recovery legislation of the republic to the south of us. One cause that brought about governmental action to help the farmers there was the

Farm Loan Act-Mr. McIntosh
disparity between agricultural and industrial prices. That disparity became very serious and action had to be taken. Legislation followed by congress adopting the administrative agricultural act and the industrial recovery act. Another cause was that the spread in prices between agricultural and industrial products broke the purchasing power of the nation and as a result the credit structure of the whole country was interfered with.
The same thing is really the cause of the resolution before the house so far as Canada is concerned. The time has come in the history of this dominion when one of our basic institutions, agriculture, as we have heard to-night on all sides, is in a serious plight, just as it was across the border, and action has had to be taken. I am not one to say that the government ought to be blamed because that action has been somewhat belated because I am one of those who believe that it is better late than never; even a deathbed repentance is good if out of it can grow some constructive action that is helpful to others, although the government repenting may not be saved. So I say that I have been pleased to see the pleasant features that have characterized this debate. It has proved at least one thing: that we can have a debate in this house in a cooperative spirit. That is, we can agree on some things. To my mind that is indicative of parliamentary progress and also an honour to members of this chamber.
A great deal of interest has been shown in this debate and we know in a psychological sense interest always arouses attention, attention arouses action and action is always typical of the character of the individual. There can be no disputing that fact. That is sound individual economy. The same thing holds true as to this resolution. The interest in the house has been satisfactory and a good deal of attention has been aroused. The whole matter now will depend upon the action by the government and the character of that action during the next year or two. In other words, the whole success of this measure will depend upon the machinery established by the government and the way in which the work is carried out. If the machinery established is unworkable and not guided by a wise personnel, then of course the results will not be as anticipated, but I am hopeful that the results will be very good and so far as the resolution is concerned I believe the more adaptable the legislation that will grow out of it, the greater the success that will characterize the government's move.
The resolution deals with facilitating and extending credit to farmers, purchasing additional bonds issued by the board and guaranteed by the government, and amending the constitution of the board. These three parts of the resolution look hopeful and lead me to believe the government back of them is sincere about it and that we may look for ameliorative action during the next year or two.
I am pleased also to notice that parallel or concurrent legislation is under way in the different parts of Canada and that the measure will be a national piece of legislation; that is, it will apply to all Canada and not to a part of it. As a member from the west, and particularly from Saskatchewan, I am gratified to know Saskatchewan will be able to take advantage of this legislation. So far as the riding I have the honour to represent is concerned I may say that during the last two years we have had splendid crops; perhaps some of the best crops in Canada were in northern Saskatchewan last year. I do not care where you may go for comparison. Notwithstanding that I believe there will be great work to do for this measure when it becomes operative and therefore I am taking advantage of the debate to-night to say a few words on its behalf.
The two main features of the resolution are: first getting debts adjusted, and, second, extending credit. The whole essence of the legislation depends upon these two features of the legislation. So far as adjustment of debts is concerned, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act of 1934 has not as yet covered a great deal of ground in Saskatchewan. I was speaking to the official receiver in the North Battleford area and he gave me to understand that only about twenty to twenty-five per cent of the debts before him were adjusted. Even twenty or twenty-five per cent means something, but that would leave about seventy-five per cent of the debts untouched and that means that in connection with seventy-five per cent of the debts coming before him for adjustment he found it impossible to get any adjustment. He said that he lacked power; he was chairman of a committee of three as it were; the creditor's, representative was there, the debtor was there and he was there himself, and if they did not come to an agreement, nothing could be done. Consequently in seventy-five per cent of the cases no agreement was reached and the debt adjustment was passed on to the provincial board of review. The Saskatchewan board did not

Mr. Speaker, I would like to associate myself with hon. members in all quarters of the house in commending the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) for bringing down this resolution. Representing as I do an agricultural constituency in Ontario I am heartily in sympathy with the proposal and commend the government for at least making some move in regard to reduction of interest on money loaned to farmers.

Some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-night have said they thought this legislation has been brought down too late. While I confess it would have been better for the great basic industry of this country, agriculture, if the government had brought down this legislation two or three years ago, yet I am glad that they did bring it down in the last session. As far as I am concerned I want to go on record as saying that I will support this legislation and be whiling to give credit to the government for bringing it down. To the Minister of Finance I say I think it will be a great mistake and a serious hardship upon the farmers of this country-I speak more particularly for the farmers in my own constituency in w'estern Ontario

if the rate of interest is not brought down to at most four per cent. If I understood the minister correctly this afternoon he stated that the cost of administration of this act would probably be about one and a half to two per cent, which would increase the rate of interest. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unfortunately we are not in committee. I made the suggestion earlier that it might have been wiser to go into committee where we could have had question and answer. I should like to have risen several times, but under the rules I could not. But when we get into committee I shall be glad to answer as many questions as I can.

I thank the minister
for his courtesy. But may I say that there has been no legislation attempted in this parliament during the last four or five years to aid the farmers. I know I may be getting very close to a discussion that would be controversial, and I do not want to do that; nevertheless, except perhaps for the attempt to get further markets for farmers and better prices, that is my opinion. I am free to admit that in the last year or two there has been a slight increase in the prices of some commodities that the farmer grows; wheat, for instance, has advanced a good deal over two years ago; the price of hogs has advanced, and so on. But even to-day the basic industry of Ontario is in dire distress. If, therefore, there is any possibility of bringing the cost of administration of this act down, the minister should do so. I go further and say that if it is not possible to bring it down so that the rate charged may not exceed four per cent, then anything above that the government and the country should pay. I say that for this reason: the farmer gets no benefit from unemployment insurance. As

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Sanderson
to unemployment insurance let me say that if the bill when it comes in meets with the approval of the opposition, speaking only for myself, I shall be glad to support it. But it affords relief only to certain classes of workers. So far as the farmer is concerned it will cost him something and he will get nothing. Even, therefore, if the cost of administration of this proposed legislation for the relief of the farmers is considerable, I think the government should bear that charge so that the rate of interest shall not be over four per cent. That would go a long way towards helping the farmers of th'is country.
I do not know whether the Minister of Finance is familiar with the plight of the farmers in Ontario, which is a great agricultural province. The part of the province from which I come, and the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this house, in normal times is one of the most prosperous farming communities in Ontario.
I want to point out to the minister that with few exceptions farmers who a few years ago were in a comfortable position, with either no mortgages or small mortgages on their farms, and in many cases with resources laid up in the way of investments or money in the bank, now find themselves right up against it. In almost every case the resources which were laid up for a rainy day have disappeared. I am not going to blame that condition on this government, but it is a condition that exists. If the government knew t]ie plight of the farmers in this province and understood their difficulties they would realize that unless a rate of interest of four per cent or less is secured on loans to farmers, this legislation will not be of much help.
This afternoon the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) read some statistics with regard to the earnings of farmers throughout the dominion. If I understood him correctly the hon. member said that for the calendar year 1933 the average earning of the farmer amounted to something over $600, while in 1934 that average had increased to something over S700. How is a farmer with a family, with a mortgage on his farm and with taxes to pay, to navigate financially with an income of less than S80O a year? I quite agree with the statement made by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. Golding), that if the basic industry is not prosperous there can be no prosperity for anyone. The farmers have the buying power; they have the largest spending power of any industry in Canada, and when that spending power is curtailed or almost cut off, as it has been for the last four or five years, they find themselves in dire distress. So I would urge the Minister of
Finance to do everything possible to get the rate of interest down to four per cent.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that in the county from which I come many farms that have been perhaps handed down from father to son, or owned by the one family for many years, have been practically taken away during the last four years because the farmers have been unable to pay either the interest or the principal of the mortgages. If you go around the rural sections of Ontario, and particularly western Ontario, you will find many vacant, deserted farms, with taxes and interest arrears accumulating, representing a condition that is almost intolerable. If this legislation will give the farmers any relief I am all for it, no matter what may be the cost of administering the act. Just here I might say to the minister and to the government, in regard to the cost of administration, that the governmental machinery of this country is too expensive. In almost every department there is duplication as between the federal and provincial governments, which only adds to the cost. I am not saying this in a critical or offensive way, but there are too many members of the outside civil service travelling up and down the country. It is costing too much money, and in the final analysis the consumer has to pay for it. In connection with this legislation the minister might well set a good example by not having too many officials and thus curtailing the expense of administration.
I do not think I have a great deal more to say, Mr. Speaker. Local boards were referred to several times this afternoon. In my opinion the setting up of local boards will only add unnecessary expense, and if it would mean any saving I would recommend that the minister cut out the local boards in order to reduce expenses to the bone and set a good example to the other departments.
There is just one other point to which I should like to refer. I said many farms in the province of Ontario were vacant, but there is another side to the question that I do not think has been considered as yet. Back in 1918, 1919 and 1920, when conditions were what we called prosperous, when farmers were receiving big prices for everything they had to sell and when trade and commerce was expanding-and expenses were expanding as well-many well to do farmers in my part of the country, like other business men of that period, branched out and added a second and in some instances a third farm at prices at least double what they would have to pay to-day. In almost every case they had to borrow money and give a mortgage covering not only the second or third farm but also

Farm Loan Act-Mr. Boulanger
their home farm. To-day those men are in a terrible condition. They have not sufficient income to pay the interest on the mortgage, and they are loaded up with farm property on which, in many instances, they could not realize twenty-five per cent of the cost. I mention this to indicate to the minister the condition of the farmers in old Ontario, and :o show that they need some assistance from this government. I hope this measure is only the beginning of the assistance that will be rendered by the government to the agriculturists of the province of Ontario.
Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-ihasse): Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house for more than a moment. I really cannot take part in this debate because I was not in the house when the resolution was presented and explained; I was not here because I was attending the sitting of the royal commission on price spreads.
I should like to refer for a moment, however, to something said this evening by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). If I understood the hon. gentleman aright- md if I did not he will correct me-he blamed the government of Quebec for not having passed enabling legislation in connection with the amendments made to the farm loan act last session. I hold no brief for the Quebec government, but I think it only fair to say that one of the main amendments of last year, in fact the only important amendment, concerned the second mortgage that might be secured by a person who had already received a loan from the farm loan board. The amendment provided that the second mortgage could be secured on the land, live stock or other personal property of the farmer. Of course the hon. member for Dorchester knows very well that in the province of Quebec, under our legal system, there is no mortgage on personal property, on live stock or on chattels. A chattel mortgage is unknown in that province. Perhaps that was the reason the Quebec government did not pass enabling legislation to put into force in the province of Quebec the amendments made to the Canadian Farm Loan Act at the last session.

Mr. Speaker, unless the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act are made supplementary neither piece of legislation will be as great a benefit to the farmer as was originally anticipated. I understand the mortgage indebtedness on farms in this country to-day is about 8700,000,000. I suppose most of that sum will be readjusted under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and if it is not

it should be. In view of the fact that there is such a huge mortgage indebtedness in Canada-
Is it all on farms?

Yes, on farms only. In view of that fact I am quite convinced we shall certainly require more than the original 815,000,000 voted in this chamber, and I venture to say we will need even more than the $90,000,000 spoken of to-night. The government should be congratulated, however, upon increasing the amount from $40,000,000 to $90,000,000, because the farmers will be benefited at least doubly thereby.
Just 'before I left for Ottawa I met a farmer in my district who told me that provided he paid his indebtedness to the mortgage company they were willing to reduce his debt by thirty-five per cent. The nigger in the woodpile lies in the fact that he is absolutely unable to get credit to discharge that indebtedness. The only way he could get it would be through the farm loan board, at a lower rate of interest and on more reasonable terms. I agree with hon. members who say that the interest rates should be reduced to four per cent. Very few people realize what a reduction of one per cent means to a farmer; in many cases it means the difference between success and failure. I believe these two pieces of legislation should be complementary, otherwise the farmers will not derive from them the benefit that they should.

Mr. Speaker,
in the few moments at my disposal
Has the hon. member for Queens spoken before?

No, not on this question. I am sorry to have to speak now, and I can assure hon. members I should have had no notion in the world of doing so had it not been for one remark made by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), a remark which to my way of thinking was not only contrary to the facts but was quite unfair.
He said that during the last four years there had not been a single thing done in this House of Commons to aid the farmers. I like to see a debate conducted on a fair and square plan. I recall the very first act of this government, at the first session, was to pave the way for the Ottawa conference agreements. I have in my mind, too, legislation for debt adjustments, the marketing act and the wheat bonus.

Will the hon. member permit a question?

The hon. member has
spoken. Almost everything that has been done in this House of Commons during the life of this parliament has been done with the aim and object of aiding our farmers. Let me say further that I do not know of one piece of legislation passed by this government to aid farmers which was not strenuously opposed by almost every member on the opposite side of the house.
The hon. member made his speech last night on the Ottawa agreements.

I did not speak last night on this motion, and I have the right to say something at the present time. The hon. member who has just interrupted is one of the worst objectors in the house; he objects to everything which would benefit or alleviate conditions under which the farmers are operating.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bury in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had hoped that we could introduce the bill to-night and thus avoid practically a week's delay. I have sat here for six solid hours and have not had an opportunity to say a word, because according to the rules I have no right to reply on the motion to go into committee. I am making no complaint; I am merely stating that I feel it my duty to reply to certain observations which have been made. Under the circumstances I shall move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
